messages.content: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test catches 99% of cases and wrongly flags 1% of healthy people. If I test positive, what's the chance I actually have it? My gut says about 99%.

Your gut is doing what almost everyone's does: it hears "99% accurate" and stops there. The missing ingredient is how rare the disease is. Count actual people instead of percentages.

Imagine 100,000 people take the test.

- 100 of them have the disease (1 in 1,000). The test catches 99% of them, so 99 test positive.
- 99,900 are healthy. The test wrongly flags 1% of them: 999 false positives.
- Total positives: 99 + 999 = 1,098.

Of those 1,098 positive results, only 99 are real. 99 / 1,098 is about 9% — roughly 1 in 11.

The test didn't get worse; the disease is just so rare that even a small false-alarm rate, applied to a huge healthy majority, produces ten false alarms for every true catch. This is why a positive on a screening test is the start of a workup, not a diagnosis: the second, confirmatory test is where the real sorting happens.

My email filter catches 99% of spam and only sends 1% of good mail to the junk folder. Roughly how much of my junk folder is actually spam? I get about 1,000 emails a month and maybe 100 of them are spam.

Work it with your own numbers: 1,000 emails, 100 spam, 900 legitimate.

- Of the 100 spam messages, the filter catches 99% — 99 land in junk.
- Of the 900 good messages, it wrongly sends 1% — 9 land in junk.
- Junk folder total: 99 + 9 = 108 messages, of which 99 are spam.

99 / 108 is about 92%. So roughly 9 out of 10 messages in your junk folder really are spam, and about 1 in 12 is a good message worth rescuing.

Notice the contrast with a rare-disease test using the exact same 99%/1% accuracy: there, a positive meant only a 9% chance of being real. The difference is the base rate — spam is 10% of your mail, not 0.1%. Same filter quality, completely different meaning for a flag, because what got flagged started out common instead of rare.
I got called back after a routine mammogram and I'm frightened. The nurse said callbacks are common and usually nothing. Can you show me the numbers so I understand what a callback actually means?

First: a callback is genuinely common, and "usually nothing" is accurate, not a brush-off. Here is the shape of the numbers, using round figures close to typical screening programs.

Out of 1,000 women screened:

- About 100 get called back for more imaging. That's 1 in 10 — if you've had several mammograms, being called back at least once is more normal than not.
- Of those 100 callbacks, about 95 turn out to be nothing: a shadow, overlapping tissue, a cyst — cleared by the extra pictures or a short follow-up.
- About 5 of the 100 are found to have cancer.

So a callback carries roughly a 5-in-100 chance of being cancer, and a 95-in-100 chance of ending with "all clear." The program accepts 95 false alarms because the alternative — only calling back obvious cases — would miss cancers while they're smallest and most treatable.

None of this makes the waiting easy, and it isn't a promise about your result; only your follow-up imaging can give that. Do go to the appointment promptly, and if the anxiety is heavy, tell the clinic — they hear it constantly and can often schedule you sooner. But the callback itself is the system being cautious, not the system having found something.

My employer drug-tests everyone. The test is supposed to be 95% sensitive and 98% specific, and they say about 2% of the workforce uses the drug. If someone tests positive, how likely is it they're actually a user?

Count a workforce of 1,000.

- 2% use the drug: 20 people. The test catches 95% of them: 19 true positives (and 1 user slips through).
- 980 don't use it. Specificity 98% means 2% of them are wrongly flagged: about 20 false positives (0.02 x 980 = 19.6, call it 20).
- Total positive results: 19 + 20 = 39.

Only 19 of the 39 positives are real users — about half. A positive result on this test is roughly a coin flip.

That's not an argument the test is useless; it's an argument for what good programs actually do: treat the first positive as a screening result, then confirm with a more precise laboratory test before anyone's job is on the line. The math says the screen alone convicts about as many innocent people as guilty ones, purely because users are rare and the test is applied to everyone.
A stadium uses facial recognition that's 99% accurate to spot 10 banned people in a crowd of 50,000. Security gets an alert. How likely is it to be one of the 10?

Give the system its best case: it catches all 10 banned people. Now count the false alarms.

- Crowd: 50,000 people, of whom 49,990 are innocent.
- The system wrongly matches 1% of innocent faces: 0.01 x 49,990 is about 500 false alerts.
- Total alerts: 10 real + 500 false = 510.

So a given alert has about a 10 / 510 chance — roughly 2% — of being one of the banned ten. Security would chase about 51 alerts for every genuinely banned person, and 98% of the people they stop would be innocent fans.

"99% accurate" sounds decisive until you apply the 1% error to a crowd where the targets are 0.02% of the people. Rare targets plus huge crowds means the false alarms win by sheer numbers, every time.

Following up on screening tests: if a first test leaves me at about a 9% chance of having a rare disease (1 in 1,000 base rate, test 99% sensitive, 1% false alarms), what does a second positive on an independent repeat test do to that chance?

Take the people who tested positive the first time and run the same numbers on just them. From 100,000 people, the first round produced 1,098 positives: 99 with the disease, 999 without.

Now test those 1,098 again with an independent test of the same quality:

- Of the 99 who have it, 99% test positive again: 98 people.
- Of the 999 who don't, 1% are unlucky twice: about 10 people.
- Double positives: 98 + 10 = 108, of whom 98 are real.

98 / 108 is about 91%. Two positives move you from 9% to roughly 91% — the second test is powerful precisely because the first one already filtered out the vast healthy majority, so the false-alarm rate now applies to a small group instead of 99,900 people.

Two cautions. "Independent" matters: if both tests make the same mistake on the same sample (same lab method, same cross-reacting substance), the errors correlate and the real gain is smaller. And 91% is still not certainty — it's why doctors layer a different kind of test next rather than repeating the same one forever.

A crime lab says a DNA profile matches only 1 in 100,000 random people. Police trawled a database covering a city of 2,000,000 and got one hit — the defendant. The prosecutor says the match means there's a 99.999% chance he's the source. What's wrong with that?

The prosecutor has the probability facing backwards. "1 in 100,000" is the chance a random innocent person matches. It is not the chance this defendant is innocent given the match.

Count the city. If the real source were not in the database at all, how many innocent matches would the trawl be expected to turn up anyway?

2,000,000 people / 100,000 = 20 expected matches.

So a database this size should produce about 20 matching profiles by chance alone. The police found one and stopped — but the match by itself puts the defendant in a pool of roughly 20 equally-matching people, only one of whom is the source. On the DNA alone, that's closer to a 1-in-20 suspicion than 99.999% certainty.

This error has a name: the prosecutor's fallacy. The fix isn't to throw the evidence out — a match is a strong lead. It's to combine it honestly: if other evidence (presence in the city that night, opportunity, no alibi) narrows the 20 down, the DNA then multiplies that smaller suspicion into something powerful. What it can't do is carry the whole case by itself when it was found by searching two million people.
A home test kit advertises "95% accurate." How can a test be 95% accurate and still have its positive results be wrong half the time?

Because "accuracy" blends two different errors into one number, and the blend hides the one you care about. Watch it happen with 1,000 people, where 50 have the condition (5%).

Say the test:

- catches 45 of the 50 cases (90% sensitivity), missing 5;
- correctly clears 902 of the 950 healthy people (about 95% specificity), wrongly flagging 48.

Overall correct calls: 45 + 902 = 947 out of 1,000 — about 95% accurate, as advertised.

But look only at the positives: 45 real + 48 false = 93 positive results, and just 45 / 93 — about 48% — are true. If you test positive, it's a coin flip, from a "95% accurate" test.

The trick is that healthy people dominate the count, so getting them mostly right inflates the headline number. Whenever a test quotes one accuracy figure, ask for the two separate ones — how often it catches cases, and how often it cries wolf — and then ask how common the condition is in people like you. Those three numbers, not the blend, tell you what your result means.

A startup says its interview screening tool "predicts job success with 80% accuracy," and they want us to use it to filter applicants. About 10% of our applicants would actually succeed in the role. Should we be impressed?

Run their filter over 100 applicants and see what comes out the other side.

- 10 would actually succeed. An 80%-sensitive screen flags 8 of them — and rejects 2 good hires before a human ever sees them.
- 90 would not succeed. If the screen also wrongly passes 30% of them, that's 27 people flagged as promising who aren't.
- The "promising" pile: 8 + 27 = 35 people, of whom 8 would succeed — about 23%.

So the tool turns a pool with a 10% success rate into a pool with a 23% success rate. That's a real improvement — you'd interview a richer pile — but it's nowhere near "80% accurate" as a hiring oracle, and it silently discards 1 in 5 of your best candidates at the door.

The question to ask the vendor is which accuracy they mean: the rate at which it catches successes, the rate at which it rejects failures, or the blended number, which mostly reflects how many failures there were to reject. With rare successes, the blended number always flatters the tool.

Our store's camera AI flags suspected shoplifters. On a typical day 2,000 people shop and maybe 4 actually steal. The vendor says the system catches 90% of thefts and only flags 0.5% of honest shoppers. Is a flag worth a guard's attention?

Count one day.

- 4 shoplifters: the system catches 90% of them, so about 3.6 — call it 3 or 4 real flags a day.
- 1,996 honest shoppers: 0.5% wrongly flagged is 0.005 x 1,996, about 10 false flags a day.
- Total flags: roughly 14, of which about 4 are real.

So around 1 flag in 4 — 29% — is an actual theft in progress. Whether that's "worth it" depends on what a flag triggers. If it quietly tells a guard to keep an eye on someone, a 1-in-4 hit rate is usable. If it means confronting or detaining a shopper, then 10 innocent people a day get accused — an expensive policy in every sense.

The vendor's two percentages are honest; they're just not the number you act on. You act on the composition of the flag pile, and that is set by how rare shoplifting is compared to shopping. Any detection system aimed at rare behavior lives or dies on that ratio, not on its accuracy claims.
Our company has 200 employees and one of them took money from a register. HR bought a "99% accurate" lie detector test and wants to test everyone. I'm suspicious of this plan. Am I right?

You are. Run the test over your 200 people, giving it the best possible behavior — assume it definitely flags the thief.

- 1 thief: flagged. Good.
- 199 innocent employees: the test wrongly flags 1% of them, and 0.01 x 199 is about 2 people.

So the test hands HR a list of about 3 names: the thief and roughly 2 innocent colleagues, with no way to tell which is which. Two people's reputations get burned to catch one thief — and that's the optimistic version, since real polygraph-style tests perform far worse than 99% and their errors aren't random in a tidy way.

The general rule: the rarer the thing you're hunting, the more your results are dominated by false accusations, no matter how accurate the test sounds. Screening everyone for something only one person did is the worst possible setup for it.

A baseball scout told me his physical test identifies future pros: it's right about 90% of the time on the kids who make it, and only 2% of the kids who won't make it pass. My son passed. Out of 10,000 kids tested, maybe 10 become pros. Should we be celebrating?

Celebrate the pass — it's genuinely good news — but let the numbers set the size of the party. Run 10,000 kids through it.

- 10 future pros: the test passes 90% of them, so 9 pros pass.
- 9,990 who won't make it: 2% pass anyway. 0.02 x 9,990 is about 200 kids.
- Total passes: 9 + 200 = 209.

Your son is now in a group of 209 passers that contains 9 future pros: his chance went from 1 in 1,000 (the original 10 out of 10,000) to about 9 in 209, roughly 1 in 23, or 4%.

That's a forty-fold improvement in his odds, which is real and worth something — the test works. But 96% of the kids who pass still won't make it, because being a future pro is so rare that even a small false-pass rate among ordinary kids floods the passing group. The test narrowed the field; it didn't pick the winners.

I'm reading about a screening program for a serious cancer. The brochure says it "finds cancer early" but a critic says most positive results are false alarms and many people get biopsies for nothing. Can both be right? Use simple numbers.

Yes — and with screening, they usually are both right at once. Take a stylized program with round numbers shaped like real ones. Screen 1,000 people repeatedly over ten years.

- 120 of them get at least one positive result in that decade.
- Of those 120, follow-up finds cancer in 6.
- The other 114 positives were false alarms — but each one meant extra scans, and many meant a biopsy, plus weeks of worry.

So the positive predictive value is 6 / 120 = 5%: nineteen of every twenty positive results are false alarms, and the critic's arithmetic is correct.

And the brochure can also be correct: among the 6 real cases, some were caught at a stage where treatment works far better. The honest argument about screening is never "does it find cancer early" (it does) versus "are there false alarms" (there are, in bulk). It's whether the benefit to the few — counted just as concretely, in outcomes per 1,000 people — outweighs biopsies, anxiety, and over-treatment spread across the many. Anyone arguing from only one side of that ledger is selling you half the numbers.
Teach me the odds form of Bayes' rule using a medical test, and show me it gives the same answer as counting people. Disease prevalence 1%, test sensitivity 99%, false positive rate 1%.

Two routes, same destination. First, counting people — 10,000 of them.

- 1% have the disease: 100 people. The test catches 99% of them: 99 positives.
- 9,900 don't have it. A 1% false positive rate flags 99 of them.
- Positives total 99 + 99 = 198, half of them real. A positive means a 50% chance.

Now the odds route, which compresses that into one multiplication.

- Prior odds: 1% is 1 to 99 against — for every 1 person with the disease, 99 without.
- The test's likelihood ratio: how much more likely a positive is in a sick person than a healthy one = 99% / 1% = 99. A positive result is 99 times as likely if you're sick.
- Posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio = (1 : 99) x 99 = 1 : 1.

Odds of 1 : 1 is a 50% chance — exactly what the head-count gave. The counting method is slower but impossible to fool yourself with; the odds method is what clinicians actually use at speed. One warning for the odds form: the likelihood ratio must come from the test's real sensitivity and false positive rate, and the prior has to be the prevalence in people like the patient — a test result never floats free of who was tested.
Headline: "Common food additive DOUBLES your risk of a rare cancer!" Should I throw out everything in my pantry?

Find the number the headline is standing on. "Doubles" is a relative change; it tells you nothing until you know what got doubled. For a genuinely rare cancer, the baseline might be about 1 case per 1,000,000 people per year.

Doubling that gives 2 per 1,000,000 per year. The increase — the part that could actually happen to anyone — is 1 extra case per million people per year.

Scale it to a city of 500,000: expected cases go from 0.5 a year to 1 a year. That's the whole effect, citywide.

None of this proves the additive is safe or that regulators shouldn't act — small risks multiplied over millions of people can still matter to public health. But for your pantry decision, the honest sentence is: "this might raise my annual risk from one-in-a-million to two-in-a-million." Whenever a headline shouts a multiplier, your first question should be: multiplied from what? A doubled tiny number is usually still a tiny number.
A drug ad says "cuts heart attack risk by 50%!" The fine print mentions a trial. How do I figure out what that means for an actual person?

The 50% is relative — it compares the two groups in the trial to each other. You need the trial's raw counts to get the absolute effect, which is the one a person experiences. Suppose the trial enrolled 10,000 people per group and ran for the stated period:

- Placebo group: 40 heart attacks out of 10,000 — a risk of 0.4%.
- Drug group: 20 out of 10,000 — a risk of 0.2%.

Relative reduction: 20 is half of 40, hence "50%." Absolute reduction: 0.4% - 0.2% = 0.2 percentage points — 20 fewer events per 10,000 people treated.

There's a third number doctors use, the number needed to treat: 10,000 / 20 = 500. You'd treat 500 people for the trial's duration to prevent one heart attack; the other 499 take the drug, with its costs and side effects, without that particular benefit (for this outcome, in this period).

The ad's 50% and the 0.2-point figure are the same data. One is chosen to sound large; the other tells you the size of what you'd actually be buying. Always hunt for the two raw counts — events in each group, and how many people in each group — because every honest version of the claim can be rebuilt from them.
The news says assaults near campus are "up 200%" this year. That sounds terrifying. The article mentions last year there were 3. What am I missing?

You're missing the base the percentage grew from — and the article buried it because 3 is a much less scary number than 200%.

"Up 200%" means the increase equals twice the original: 3 + (2 x 3) = 9 incidents this year. (Going from 3 to 9 is tripling; the increase itself, 6, is 200% of 3.)

So the real story is: incidents rose from 3 to 9 in a year, in an area with thousands of students. That may still be worth attention — six more people were assaulted, and a trend matters — but it's a different emotional object than "up 200%," which your brain reads as an explosion.

Small counts produce giant percentages because each single incident is worth 33% all by itself. One fewer incident and the headline would have been "up 167%"; one more, "up 233%." When the counts are this small, percentages are basically noise wearing a costume. Ask for the two counts, always: from how many, to how many.
Two headlines about the same vaccine: "Serious side effect risk TRIPLES after vaccination" and "Vaccination prevents 180 cases per 100,000." A friend says one of them must be lying. Are they?

Both can be — and here are — the same data. Put both claims on the same denominator, per 100,000 people.

The benefit side: without vaccination, about 200 per 100,000 get the disease in a season; with it, about 20 per 100,000. Cases prevented: 180 per 100,000. That's also a 90% relative reduction, but the absolute count is what matters.

The harm side: a serious side effect occurs in about 1 per 100,000 unvaccinated people (background rate) and about 3 per 100,000 vaccinated people. 1 to 3 is indeed a tripling — a 200% relative increase. In absolute terms it's 2 extra cases per 100,000.

Now the two headlines sit on one scale: 180 cases prevented against 2 extra serious side effects, per 100,000 people. You can still argue about severity, about who bears the risk, about mandates — those are values questions. But arithmetically there's no contradiction: a large relative increase in a very rare harm can coexist with a large absolute benefit. The trick to spot is the units: harm quoted as a multiplier, benefit quoted as a count. Convert everything to "per 100,000 people" and the fog lifts.
My doctor mentioned a medication with "NNT of 100" and said there's also a number needed to harm of 50 for a minor side effect. I nodded like I understood. I did not understand.

Both numbers translate trial results into people, which is exactly the right way to think about them.

NNT — number needed to treat — of 100 means: in the trial, out of every 100 people who took the drug for the study period, 1 had the bad outcome prevented who would otherwise have had it. The underlying counts might look like this: 5 events per 100 people on placebo, 4 per 100 on the drug. The difference, 1 per 100, flips into NNT = 100.

So of 100 people taking it: 1 is directly helped on this outcome, and 99 take it without that benefit — most of them were never going to have the event anyway, and a few have it despite the drug.

NNH — number needed to harm — of 50 means the side effect showed up in 2 extra people per 100 treated (say 2 per 100 on the drug versus 0 per 100 on placebo). Treat 100 people: expect about 2 cases of the side effect.

Putting your numbers together over 100 patients: 1 serious event prevented, about 2 minor side effects caused. Whether that's a good trade depends on how bad the prevented event is versus how annoying the side effect is — a judgment call, but now it's a judgment call with the real quantities on the table. That translation, from percentages into "out of 100 people like me," is the single most useful trick for medical decisions.
My bank emailed: "We're raising your savings rate by 0.5%!" Then a news site said the bank "raised rates 25%." One of them is playing games. Which?

Neither is lying; they're using two different rulers, and each picked the one that suits it.

Say your rate was 2% and is now 2.5%.

- The bank's version: the rate rose by 0.5 percentage points — 2.5 - 2 = 0.5. True, and it sounds tiny.
- The news version: the increase relative to the old rate is 0.5 / 2 = 25%. Also true, and it sounds dramatic.

What lands in your account: on $10,000, a year of interest goes from $200 to $250. Fifty extra dollars.

The vocabulary fix: when the thing being measured is itself a percentage, changes come in two flavors — percentage points (the simple subtraction) and percent change (relative to the starting value). Confusing them is the oldest trick in financial and political writing. When you see a rate change quoted, ask "points or percent?" and then convert to dollars or people, whichever is real to you.
Our mayor is bragging that crime in one neighborhood "fell 30%" last year. A critic says it's spin. The neighborhood had 10 reported incidents the year before. Who's right?

Both are describing the same three incidents.

30% down from 10 is 7 — so the neighborhood went from 10 reported incidents to 7. The mayor's percentage is arithmetically true.

The critic's point is about what small numbers do to percentages. Each single incident in this neighborhood is worth 10% all by itself. If next year goes back from 7 to 10, the headline will be "crime surges 43%" (3 / 7 = 43%) — a scarier number than this year's 30%, produced by exactly the same three incidents moving in the other direction. Percentages on tiny bases are asymmetric and jumpy: down 30%, then up 43%, lands you exactly where you started.

With counts this small, one family moving away, one bar closing earlier, or one officer's patrol route can swing the "trend." The honest report is the counts themselves — 10, then 7 — plus a few years of history to see whether 7 is a change or just the wobble that single-digit numbers always have.
A scratch card advertises "50% more chances to win!" The old card gave a prize on about 2% of tickets. What does the new one actually give me?

That "50% more" multiplies the old chance; it doesn't add 50 points to it.

Old chance: 2% — on average 2 winning tickets out of every 100.
New chance: 2% x 1.5 = 3% — 3 winning tickets out of every 100.

So the improvement, in the units you'd actually experience, is one extra winning ticket per hundred bought. If you buy 100 of the old cards you expect about 2 prizes; 100 of the new, about 3.

The ad is technically truthful and practically misleading, which is the standard shape of relative claims. Also note what it doesn't say: anything about prize sizes. A card can offer more, smaller prizes — more "chances to win," less money when you do. Chance of winning and expected value are different numbers, and advertisers will always quote whichever one is prettier.

A study says a certain exposure "doubles the risk" of a disease. My 30-year-old friend is panicking; her 70-year-old father shrugged. A doctor friend says both reactions are roughly rational. How can that be?

Because "doubles" multiplies whatever your starting risk is, and their starting risks are nowhere near each other's.

Say the disease's yearly risk at age 30 is about 1 in 10,000. Doubled: 2 in 10,000. The increase is 1 extra case per 10,000 people — for your friend, a change from 0.01% to 0.02%.

At 70, say the baseline is 1 in 100. Doubled: 2 in 100. The increase is 1 extra case per 100 people — a hundred times larger in absolute terms than the same doubling at 30.

Same headline, same relative risk of 2, wildly different personal stakes. Your friend's panic is out of proportion to her 0.01-point increase; her father's shrug is arguably under-reacting to a full extra case per hundred.

This is why a relative risk quoted without an age or a baseline is almost information-free. The complete sentence is always: "risk goes from X to Y for people like you, over this period." Insist on all three parts — from, to, and for whom.
An ad for a beach umbrella says it "cuts your sunburn risk in half." Is that a big deal or marketing fluff?

It's a real effect stated in the most flattering unit. Translate it into a day at the beach.

Suppose that without shade, about 40 out of 100 fair-skinned beachgoers end the day sunburned. Cutting the risk in half means about 20 out of 100 get burned. So the umbrella saves roughly 20 sunburns per 100 beach days — for a family of four on a week's holiday, that's the difference between expecting one or two miserable, peeling evenings and probably none.

That is a genuinely worthwhile effect — and notice it only became clear when converted from "half" into counts of people. The same phrasing on a different baseline would be fluff: if the unshaded risk were 2 in 100, halving it saves 1 sunburn per 100 days, and the ad would sound identical.

"Half the risk" is a shape, not a size. The size is always: from how many, to how many, out of how many.
Our CEO announced "we reduced customer churn by 25%" and the board applauded. Churn was 8% last quarter. I feel like something's off. Is it?

Your instinct is right — the sentence is true and smaller than it sounds.

A 25% reduction of an 8% churn rate means churn fell by 0.25 x 8 = 2 percentage points, to 6%. Put customers on it: with 10,000 customers, last quarter 800 left; this quarter 600 left. The company kept 200 customers it would previously have lost.

Keeping 200 customers is a real achievement and may be worth a lot of money. But notice the two honest ways to say it: "churn fell 25%" (relative) and "churn fell from 8% to 6%" (absolute). The first gets applause; the second gets a follow-up question about whether 2 points is good. That's why executives reach for the relative version.

It's also why you should check the reverse move someday: if churn creeps back from 6% to 8%, that's the same 200 customers — but it will be reported, if at all, as a "2-point rise," never as "churn up 33%," even though 2 / 6 = 33% is the same arithmetic the CEO just used in the flattering direction.
A public health ad says regular screening "reduces deaths from this cancer by 20%." My uncle says screening is oversold. How do I weigh this without a medical degree?

Ask what the 20% is standing on, then weigh the full ledger per 1,000 people. The numbers below are a stylized illustration shaped like real screening debates — the method is what transfers to any specific program.

Over ten years, out of 1,000 people:

- Unscreened: 5 die of this cancer.
- Screened: 4 die of it. 5 to 4 is indeed a 20% relative reduction. In absolute terms: 1 death prevented per 1,000 people screened for a decade.
- Meanwhile, about 200 of the 1,000 get at least one false alarm along the way, leading to extra scans and biopsies, and a small number are treated for growths that would never have harmed them.

Your uncle's skepticism and the ad are both anchored in this table. The benefit is real but thin per person; the burdens are individually small but spread over hundreds of people. Whether the trade is worth it depends on the actual program's numbers, your age and risk, and how you weigh one prevented death against 200 rounds of anxiety and procedures.

What you can do without a medical degree: refuse any screening pitch — for or against — that won't give you the per-1,000 table. Benefits, false alarms, and over-treatment, all on the same denominator. Advocates who only quote the 20% are marketing; so are critics who only quote the 200.

A paper reports an odds ratio of 2.7 for a treatment and the press release says patients were "2.7 times as likely to recover." Recovery rates were 80% on the treatment and 60% on control. Is the press release right?

No — and this is one of the most reliable ways results get inflated in translation. Work with 100 patients per group.

- Treatment: 80 recover, 20 don't. The odds of recovery are 80 : 20 = 4 to 1.
- Control: 60 recover, 40 don't. Odds are 60 : 40 = 1.5 to 1.
- Odds ratio: 4 / 1.5 = 2.67 — the paper's 2.7. That number is real.

But "times as likely" describes the ratio of probabilities, not odds: 80% / 60% = 1.33. Patients were 1.33 times as likely to recover — a 20-percentage-point improvement (60% to 80%), not a near-tripling.

Odds ratios behave politely only when the outcome is rare: if recovery were 8% versus 3%, the odds ratio (about 2.8) and the risk ratio (2.67) nearly agree, because with small numbers odds and probabilities are almost the same. When the outcome is common, like 60–80%, odds stretch the ratio dramatically and the two measures split apart.

Rule of thumb: if a headline says "X times as likely," check whether the underlying statistic was an odds ratio. If it was, and the event is common, the honest multiplier is smaller — find the two raw rates and divide them yourself.
A poll of about 1,000 voters has Candidate A at 52% and Candidate B at 48%, margin of error ±3 points. The headline says "A leads." Does she?

Not in any way you should rely on. The margin of error applies to each candidate's number separately.

- A's true support is plausibly anywhere in 52 ± 3: from 49% to 55%.
- B's is plausibly 48 ± 3: from 45% to 51%.

Those ranges overlap heavily. The data is consistent with A ahead 55–45, with a dead heat, and with B actually leading 51–49. A 4-point gap measured with a ±3-point instrument is a shrug, not a lead.

Newsrooms know this and write "leads" anyway, because "statistical tie, race too close to characterize" doesn't get clicked. A useful habit: mentally replace the headline with "A at 52, B at 48, ±3" and ask whether you'd bet money on it. At these numbers, you'd be betting on noise. What would settle it is several independent polls pointing the same way — the average of polls has a much smaller effective error than any one of them.
Three polls of the same race came out this week: 47%, 52%, and 49% for the same candidate. One of them must be wrong, right? Which one?

Probably none of them is "wrong" — you're watching measurement noise, and expecting a poll to be a photograph when it's more like a weather reading.

Each poll samples about 1,000 people out of millions, so each carries a margin of error around ±3 points just from the luck of who got sampled. Read the three numbers as fuzzy estimates:

- 47 ± 3 means somewhere in 44–50.
- 52 ± 3 means 49–55.
- 49 ± 3 means 46–52.

All three ranges contain the neighborhood of 49–50, and the simple average of the three is (47 + 52 + 49) / 3 = 49.3%. The polls agree with each other far better than the headlines suggest; they jointly say "about 49 or 50, give or take a couple."

Polls also differ in method — who counts as a "likely voter," how they weight by age and education — so some spread is systematic, not just luck. The takeaway: one poll is weather, several polls averaged are climate. Judge a race by the average and the trend, never by the single most dramatic number, which is the one that will always be quoted at you.
Why do pollsters always seem to interview about 1,000 people? Why not 100, or 100,000?

Because the margin of error shrinks with the square root of the sample size, and 1,000 is where the cost-benefit curve bends. The working approximation is margin of error ≈ 1 / √n.

- n = 100: 1/√100 = 1/10 → ±10 points. Too fuzzy to distinguish 52–48 from 48–52.
- n = 400: 1/√400 = 1/20 → ±5 points.
- n = 1,000: 1/√1000 ≈ 1/31.6 → about ±3 points. Good enough for most horse-race purposes.
- n = 10,000: 1/√10000 = 1/100 → ±1 point.

Notice the cruelty of the square root: to halve the margin you must quadruple the sample. Going from 400 to 1,600 interviews buys you ±5 → ±2.5. Going from 1,000 to 10,000 — ten times the cost and effort — buys only ±3 → ±1.

So pollsters cluster near 1,000 because that's where each additional interview stops paying for itself. And a warning that comes free with the formula: it assumes the sample is genuinely random and representative. A biased sample of 100,000 is precisely, confidently wrong — the formula measures only sampling luck, not whether you asked the right people.
Big headline: "Young voters abandon Candidate A — support among under-30s crashes to 31%!" The poll interviewed 1,000 people total. What should I check before believing the youthquake?

Check how many under-30s were actually in the sample. The headline number for the whole poll hides the subgroup's size — and in a typical poll of 1,000, under-30s might be only about 120 respondents.

The margin of error for that subgroup is roughly 1 / √120 ≈ ±9 points. So the "crash to 31%" is really "somewhere between about 22% and 40%," a range wide enough to contain last month's number, no change at all, and a genuine collapse — the poll cannot tell them apart.

This is the subgroup trap, and it manufactures most dramatic demographic headlines. The full-sample margin (±3) gets printed in the article; the subgroup's real margin (±9 or worse) almost never does. Small subgroups also swing wildly between polls by pure luck, which is why "young voters surge" and "young voters abandon" stories can alternate month to month with nothing changing in the world.

Rule: before believing any claim about a slice of a poll, find the slice's n. If it's in the low hundreds, the margin is ±6 to ±10 and most of the drama is noise.
Same polling firm, same week: among all adults the race is 50–45, among registered voters 51–46, among "likely voters" 48–50. Did the voters change their minds between paragraphs?

Nobody changed their mind. The pollster changed the filter — and the filter is a guess, not a measurement.

One survey, one set of answers. Then three different sieves:

- All adults: everyone interviewed counts equally: 50–45.
- Registered voters: throw out the unregistered: 51–46.
- Likely voters: keep only those the firm's model predicts will actually vote — based on past turnout, stated enthusiasm, and similar questions: 48–50.

The likely-voter screen assumes younger and less habitual voters will stay home, so it up-weights older, regular voters, who lean differently. If the model is right, 48–50 is the best estimate of the election. If turnout surprises — a wave of first-time voters, say — the screen throws away exactly the people who decide the result, and the "all adults" number was the honest one.

Neither figure is fabricated; they're answers to different questions. "Who do adults prefer?" versus "Who will the electorate that shows up prefer?" When two polls disagree, the first thing to compare isn't the candidates' numbers — it's the sieves.
A challenger I've never heard of is polling at 12% against a famous incumbent's 55%. The challenger's campaign says the poll is actually great news for them. Spin, or is there something to it?

There's something to it, and the key number is buried in the poll's own tables: name recognition. Suppose 70% of respondents say they've never heard of the challenger.

Count 1,000 respondents:

- 700 have never heard of him — almost none of them can support a name they don't know.
- 300 know who he is.
- His 12% support is 120 people — all of them necessarily from the 300 who know him.

So among voters who know him, his support is 120 / 300 = 40%. The poll is mostly measuring his obscurity, not his appeal: his ceiling today is set by the 30% who can identify him.

That reframes the race. The incumbent's 55% is close to a settled judgment — everyone knows him. The challenger's 12% is a floor built on 30% awareness, and the campaign's real task is introductions, not persuasion. This is also why early polls in races with an unknown challenger systematically understate them: they measure the starting line as if it were the finish. The number to watch in the next poll isn't his support — it's his recognition. If that climbs to 60% and support holds at 40% of the aware, he's suddenly at 24% without converting a single new admirer.
A pollster told me they dialed 10,000 numbers to get 500 completed interviews, and the margin of error is ±4.4 points. If the math is that clean, why do polls still miss elections?

Because the margin of error only prices one kind of error — the luck of which 500 people you happened to get — and assumes the 500 are a miniature of the electorate. Look at what the response rate does to that assumption.

500 completions out of 10,000 dials is a 5% response rate. The other 9,500 people declined, didn't answer, or never picked up. If the kind of person who answers an unknown number and talks to a stranger for ten minutes differs politically from the kind who doesn't — by age, by trust in institutions, by how busy their evenings are — the sample is skewed before a single question is asked, and no amount of ±4.4 arithmetic touches that skew.

Pollsters fight it with weighting: if the sample has too few young men, each young man's answers get counted extra. That helps when the weighting variables capture the real difference. It fails when the decisive difference is something unmeasured — say, enthusiasm to vote this particular year.

So read the margin of error as a floor on the uncertainty, not the total: it says "even in a perfect world, ±4.4." The real error includes who refused, who was never reachable, and who the likely-voter model got wrong — none of which appear in the fine print.
A race is reported as "A leads B, 44% to 42%." The report barely mentions the other 14%. My friend says A is actually winning by more than it looks. Who's reading it right?

Your friend has spotted the undecideds — and there are two honest ways to present the same numbers, which tell different stories.

The raw ballot: A 44, B 42, undecided 14, out of every 100 voters. The "lead" is 2 points, well inside any margin of error.

Now look only at the 86 voters who've decided: A's share of them is 44 / 86 = 51.2%, B's is 42 / 86 = 48.8%. Among decided voters it's a 51–49 race — A is winning the voters who exist so far by a clearer margin than the headline suggests.

But the 14 undecideds get a vote too, and where they land decides everything. If they split evenly, the finish is 51–49 for A. If they break 2-to-1 for B (late deciders often break against an incumbent, or for the challenger, depending on the race), B gains about 9.3 and A about 4.7: final score roughly 51.3–48.7 for B.

So the truthful summary is: A leads among the decided, and the race belongs to the 14% who haven't chosen. Any report that quotes 44–42 without the 14 is showing you two-thirds of the picture — and the missing third is the part that moves.
A guy with a clipboard outside the mall surveyed 50 shoppers and announced "60% of shoppers love the new store layout!" My coworker is citing this in a meeting. How much is that number worth?

Run the margin: with n = 50, the margin of error is roughly 1 / √50 ≈ ±14 points.

So "60% love it" honestly means "somewhere between about 46% and 74% love it" — a range that includes "most shoppers are indifferent or worse" and "three-quarters are delighted." The survey cannot distinguish triumph from shrug.

And that's before the bigger problem: who got surveyed. Mall-intercept polls sample people who are at that mall, at that hour, willing to stop for a clipboard — a group that excludes everyone the layout already drove away. The 50 friendliest, least hurried shoppers in the building are not "shoppers."

For the meeting: the number isn't evidence of much beyond "of 50 cooperative people at the mall that day, 30 said something positive." If a decision rides on it, the cheap fix is a bigger, more varied sample — a few hundred responses collected across days and times gets the margin near ±5 and starts to mean something.
A candidate's support in monthly polls: 45, 46, 48, 49. Each poll's margin is ±3, so my brother says every one of those moves is meaningless noise and nothing is happening. Is he right?

He's right about each step and wrong about the staircase.

Individually, he's correct: 45 to 46 is well inside ±3 noise, and so is every other single step. No one poll-to-poll move here proves anything.

But look at the pattern instead of the steps. If support were truly flat, each month's reading would wobble up or down around the true value by chance — roughly a coin flip which direction. The chance of four readings marching in the same direction by luck alone is small: each step up is about a 1-in-2 shot, so three consecutive rises is about (1/2)^3 = 1 in 8, and the steady ordering 45 < 46 < 48 < 49 is more specific still. Meanwhile the endpoints differ by 4 points — 45 ± 3 (42–48) against 49 ± 3 (46–52) — and the average of all four polls, 47, is much more precisely estimated than any single one.

This is the general rule for noisy series: don't litigate individual steps; ask whether the sequence looks like a random walk around a flat line or a slow climb. Four polls rising in a row, corroborated by other pollsters, is a trend. One poll jumping 4 points is a Tuesday.
A poll's raw sample had 200 women and 800 men, but the electorate is half women. The published result differs from the raw responses. Is that the pollster cooking the numbers?

It's the pollster correcting the sample — the published number is the honest one, and here's the arithmetic so you can check.

The electorate is 500 women and 500 men per 1,000 voters. The sample has 200 women and 800 men, so each woman's response must stand for 500 / 200 = 2.5 voters, and each man's for 500 / 800 = 0.625 voters. Those multipliers are the weights.

Now suppose women support the candidate at 60% and men at 40%.

- Raw count: women contribute 0.60 x 200 = 120 supporters; men, 0.40 x 800 = 320. Raw total: 440 / 1,000 = 44%.
- Weighted: women count as 120 x 2.5 = 300; men as 320 x 0.625 = 200. Weighted total: 500 / 1,000 = 50%.

The raw 44% mostly describes the accident that men were easier to reach. The weighted 50% estimates the actual electorate. Weighting isn't cooking; refusing to weight would be.

The legitimate worry is different: weights assume the 200 women reached are typical of women generally. If the reachable ones differ from the unreachable ones in ways the weights don't capture, the correction polishes the wrong thing. Judge a poll by whether it discloses its weighting — the transparent ones are usually the careful ones.
If a poll's margin of error is ±3 and the lead is 4 points, why do statisticians say the lead itself has a bigger margin — around ±6?

Because a lead is a difference between two noisy numbers, and the noises can stack against you.

Take A at 52 ± 3 and B at 48 ± 3. The quoted 4-point lead is just the gap between the two point estimates. But A's true value could be at the low end of its range while B's is at the high end: A really at 49, B really at 51 — and the "lead" is actually a 2-point deficit. Swing the other way: A 55, B 45, a 10-point lead. The same poll is consistent with both.

In a two-candidate race the two shares are linked (if A is really lower, B is really higher), which is why the practical rule is that the margin on the gap is roughly double the headline margin: a 4-point lead with a ±3 poll carries something like ±6 of uncertainty on the gap itself. 4 ± 6 comfortably includes zero — and negative numbers.

So when a headline says "leads by 4, margin ±3," mentally rewrite it as "leads by 4 ± 6" before deciding how much it means. Leads smaller than twice the margin of error are better described as "ahead in this sample" than as "ahead".

Our campaign thinks the candidate's support moved from 50% to 53% after a debate and wants a poll to confirm the 3-point gain. The pollster says a normal 1,000-person poll can't do it and quoted us for 4,500 respondents. Is that upselling?

It's arithmetic, not upselling. To confirm a 3-point move, your measurement error has to be comfortably smaller than 3 points — say a margin of error around ±1.5.

Margin of error ≈ 1 / √n. Set it to 0.015 and solve:

√n = 1 / 0.015 ≈ 66.7, so n ≈ 66.7 x 66.7 ≈ 4,444.

Hence the quote for about 4,500. With the usual 1,000-person poll (margin ±3.1), a true 53% will routinely read as 50% or 56%, and a true 50% will read as 53% — the poll literally cannot tell the two worlds apart.

It gets worse: confirming a change means comparing two polls, and each carries its own error, so the difference is noisier than either reading. That's why professionals rarely certify a small move from a single pair of surveys; they watch several polls and the rolling average, where a real 3-point shift shows up as the whole average drifting, not one number twitching.

The honest options: pay for the big sample, accept the slower verdict of the polling average, or decide the debate worked/didn't on other evidence. What you can't do is buy a 1,000-person poll and read a 3-point move out of it — that's paying for a ruler and demanding it measure millimeters it doesn't have.
Someone told me "if a billionaire walks into a bar, everyone in it becomes a millionaire on average." Cute, but can you show me exactly how that works?

Put 10 people in the bar: 9 regulars each earning $40,000 a year, and one person earning $9,640,000 a year.

Add up all the incomes: (9 x $40,000) + $9,640,000 = $360,000 + $9,640,000 = $10,000,000.
Divide by 10 people: the mean income is exactly $1,000,000.

So the claim is literally true: the average person in the bar is a millionaire. It's also a terrible description of the bar: 9 of the 10 people in it earn $40,000, and the median income — the middle person when lined up — is $40,000.

The mean is a total divided by a count; it doesn't care how the total is shared. One enormous value can drag it anywhere. The median cares only about who's in the middle, so it's immune to the billionaire. Whenever someone quotes an "average" about money — income, house prices, wealth — ask which average. With skewed distributions, the gap between mean and median is where the truth is hiding.
The news said "average home price in our town hit $600,000," but every house I see for sale is in the low $200s. Are they making it up?

Probably not — they're reporting the mean, and a few mansions are doing heavy lifting. Imagine the last five sales in town:

$200,000, $220,000, $240,000, $260,000, and one $2,080,000 estate.

Total: $3,000,000. Mean: $3,000,000 / 5 = $600,000 — the headline number, exactly.
Median: the middle sale, $240,000 — the number matching what you're seeing.

One sale in five was atypical, and it contributed more than the other four combined ($2.08M of the $3M total). The mean dutifully reports that; it's a statement about total dollars, not about typical houses.

This is why housing statisticians usually quote the median price: half of sales above, half below, unaffected by whether a mansion happened to change hands this quarter. When a price report says "average," check whether it's mean or median before deciding the town has gone mad. A mean can jump 20% in a month because two estates sold, while the typical house didn't move at all.
The city proudly announced the "average commute is 45 minutes" and used it to design the new transit plan. Something about that bothers me but I can't name it.

What bothers you is that the average commuter may not exist. Watch: take 20 commuters.

- 10 live near work: 10-minute commutes. Total: 100 minutes.
- 10 live across the region: 80-minute commutes. Total: 800 minutes.
- Overall mean: 900 / 20 = 45 minutes.

Not one of the 20 people has anything like a 45-minute commute. The distribution has two humps — walkers and long-haulers — and the mean sits in the empty valley between them.

This is called a bimodal distribution, and it's common wherever a population is really two populations wearing one label: commutes, incomes in a company town, hospital stays, test scores in a tracked school. A transit plan designed for the fictional 45-minute rider — medium-distance routes, medium frequency — can end up serving neither the 10-minute group (who need safe sidewalks and bike lanes) nor the 80-minute group (who need express service).

Whenever an average is offered as the basis for a design or a policy, ask for the shape: a histogram, or at least the spread. A mean with no distribution is a rumor about a person who may not exist.
An airline brags that its "average flight delay is only 6 minutes." Last month my flight was delayed an hour and the departure board looked like a disaster. Can both be true?

Easily. Suppose the airline ran 100 flights last month:

- 90 departed on time: 0 minutes of delay each.
- 10 were delayed by 60 minutes each: 600 minutes of delay.
- Total delay: 600 minutes over 100 flights = a mean of 6 minutes per flight.

The brag is accurate and almost no passenger experienced it. 90% of passengers had no delay at all; 10% had an hour. The "average delay" describes the airline's total pain divided by flights — a fine operational metric — but as a prediction of your trip it's nearly useless, because delays aren't spread evenly like butter; they arrive in lumps on unlucky flights.

There's also a quiet choice in the denominator: delays averaged over all flights (including on-time ones) will always look gentler than the average delay of delayed flights — here, 60 minutes, which is the number that matters if you're deciding whether to book the tight connection.

Ask: average over what, and what's the chance of a big one? "90% on time, and when we're late it's about an hour" is the honest version of the same data.
A fund newsletter says "the average fund in our category returned 8% a year over the last decade." My broker says that number is rigged without anyone lying. How?

The rigging is survivorship: the average is computed only over funds that still exist. Reconstruct the decade with 100 funds.

- 50 funds did well enough to survive: they averaged 8% a year.
- 50 funds did badly — say they averaged 1% a year — and were quietly closed or merged away, disappearing from the category.

The newsletter's "average fund" averages the 50 survivors: 8%. The average experience of the money invested at the start, across all 100 funds, is (50 x 8 + 50 x 1) / 100 = 4.5%.

No figure was fabricated. The dead funds were simply removed from the denominator, and since funds mostly die for bad performance, removing them mechanically inflates the average. The worse the category, the more funds die, and the bigger the gap between the reported average and what investors actually earned.

The same trick runs everywhere once you see it: average returns of restaurants still open, average ratings of apps still in the store, average salaries of graduates who responded to the survey. Always ask: average of the ones that made it, or of everything that started? The graveyard is data too.
Every business book profiles college dropouts who became billionaires. My nephew now thinks dropping out is the smart move. What do the numbers actually say?

The books are sampling from the podium. Put a simple frame around it — the counts are illustrative, but the structure is the real-world one.

Imagine 10,000 students: 9,000 graduate, 1,000 drop out. Suppose this generation produces 30 billionaires:

- 3 come from the dropouts: 3 / 1,000 = 0.3% of dropouts.
- 27 come from the graduates: 27 / 9,000 = 0.3% of graduates.

Identical rates. But a book profiles people, not rates: it interviews the 3 dropout billionaires, because "dropout billionaire" is a story and "graduate billionaire" is a Tuesday. Your nephew sees 3 vivid cases and zero of the 997 dropouts who became neither billionaires nor books.

The deeper point isn't even about billionaires — almost nobody becomes one by either route. It's that the visible sample is filtered by success before you ever see it. Dropouts who failed, funds that died, bands that never got signed: they're invisible in the data you casually encounter, so your brain prices their frequency at zero.

When an argument is built from examples, ask for the denominator: how many tried this path in total, and how many of those does the example represent? 3 out of 1,000 and 3 out of 10 are opposite conclusions wearing the same anecdote.
People say "in 1800 nobody lived past 35" because average life expectancy was around 35. That can't be right — history is full of old people from back then. What's the confusion?

The confusion is between an average and a typical life. The average was dragged down by deaths in childhood, which were common then and are rare now. Make a village of 10 deaths with ages:

1, 2, 60, 65, 70, 72, 75, 78, 80, 82.

Add them: 585. Mean age at death: 585 / 10 = 58.5. Already the average says "58.5" while describing a group where 8 of 10 people lived past 60 and two died as toddlers.

Now push more infant deaths in, as 1800 had: with enough deaths at age 0–2, the mean sinks into the 30s even though anyone who survived childhood commonly lived into their 60s and 70s. The mean is doing arithmetic, not biography: every death at age 1 cancels a death at age 73 in the average, twice over.

So "life expectancy was 35" never meant "adults dropped dead at 35." It meant the average of a distribution with a brutal left tail. Old people existed in every century — they were the ones who made it through the tail. When a distribution is skewed, the mean reports the tail, and the median or the mode tells you what life actually looked like.

Two clinics report recovery rates. Clinic B: 72% of patients recover. Clinic A: only 60%. My insurer wants me at B. But a doctor friend says A is better for every kind of patient. Both can't be right... can they?

They can, and this is Simpson's paradox — the most dangerous average in statistics. Here are the full counts.

Clinic A treated 200 patients:
- Mild cases: 90 of 100 recovered = 90%.
- Severe cases: 30 of 100 recovered = 30%.
- Overall: 120 / 200 = 60%.

Clinic B treated 250 patients:
- Mild cases: 170 of 200 recovered = 85%.
- Severe cases: 10 of 50 recovered = 20%.
- Overall: 180 / 250 = 72%.

A beats B for mild cases (90% vs 85%) and for severe cases (30% vs 20%) — A is better for every kind of patient, exactly as your friend said. Yet B's overall rate is higher, because 200 of B's 250 patients (80%) were mild, while A's caseload was half severe. B's average is flattered by an easier mix of patients, not better care.

The overall rate silently answers a question nobody asked: "how did the average patient do, given this clinic's particular mix?" Your question is "how would a patient like me do?" — and that lives in the row for your kind of case. Whenever groups are compared on an overall average, check the mix. If the mixes differ, the overall number can reverse the truth in every subgroup, as it just did.
This gadget has an "average rating of 4.2 stars" from 10 reviews. I read them and nobody seems lukewarm — people either rave or shrug. What's going on?

The 4.2 is a treaty between two camps, not a consensus. One set of reviews that produces it:

- Six 5-star reviews: 6 x 5 = 30 stars.
- Four 3-star reviews: 4 x 3 = 12 stars.
- Total 42 stars over 10 reviews: 42 / 10 = 4.2.

Exactly nobody gave it 4 stars, and nobody's experience was "4.2-ish." Six buyers loved it; four found it mediocre. The average blends them into a fictional mild approval.

This pattern — a high mean built from extremes — usually means the product delights one kind of user and disappoints another: it fits small wrists, works with one phone brand, suits beginners but not pros. The useful information is in the split, not the mean. Read a couple of the 3-star reviews and ask which camp you'd fall into; their reasons will name the dividing line.

Ratings, incomes, commutes, test scores: whenever the underlying thing is really two groups, the average describes neither. A mean of 4.2 should trigger one question — what's the distribution? — and review sites that show the star histogram are giving you the real data.
A small company advertises "average pay here is $5,000 a month!" There are 20 employees. My friend works there and says almost everyone makes $3,000. Is the ad lying?

Not lying — averaging. Reconstruct the payroll:

- 19 employees at $3,000 a month: 19 x $3,000 = $57,000.
- The owner pays himself $43,000 a month.
- Total payroll: $57,000 + $43,000 = $100,000.
- Mean: $100,000 / 20 = $5,000 a month. The ad checks out.

But the median — the middle employee's pay — is $3,000, and so is the mode, the most common pay. 95% of the staff earn $3,000; the "average" employee earning $5,000 doesn't exist. One salary, the boss's, contributes 43% of the payroll and pulls the mean up by $2,000 all by itself.

Small groups make this worse: in a company of 20, a single outlier is 5% of the data. In a company of 20,000, one salary barely ripples the mean.

When a small organization quotes average pay, ask for the median, or better, the pay for the specific role you're applying for. "Average" over a skewed little group is a number about the top, dressed as a number about everyone.
A tutoring company advertises "our students improve by an average of 10 points." My daughter's tutor is fine, but should I expect her to gain 10 points?

Only if she's one of the students the program works spectacularly for. Here's a class of 30 that produces exactly that average:

- 10 students gain 30 points each: 10 x 30 = 300 points.
- 20 students gain 0 points.
- Total gain: 300 points over 30 students = an average of 10 points per student.

The advertisement is true and the median student's gain — the middle student when ranked — is 0. Two-thirds of the class got nothing measurable; a third got a transformation. The mean launders the winners' gains across everyone.

This shape is common in education and medicine alike: interventions often work very well for a subgroup (students who were behind on one specific, fixable topic, say) and barely at all for others. The average can't tell you which subgroup your daughter is in; the company probably can, if pressed — ask what fraction of students gain at least 10 points, and what distinguishes the students who gain a lot.

Better questions than "what's the average gain": What's the median? What share gain nothing? What share gain a lot? Three numbers, and the brochure's single average becomes a distribution you can actually locate your kid in.

A carnival game costs $10 to play. You draw a ball from a drum: 1 in 100 wins $1,000, otherwise you win nothing. The barker says "the average payout is $10, so it's a fair game." My wallet disagrees with the barker. Who's right?

Both of you, about different things. The barker's arithmetic is correct: the expected value is (1/100) x $1,000 + (99/100) x $0 = $10. On average, over very many plays, the game pays out $10 per $10 ticket.

But look at what actually happens when you play. Play 100 times — $1,000 of tickets — and the typical story is: 99 plays pay $0, one pays $1,000. Your median play pays nothing. The "average outcome" of $10 never occurs on any single play; it's a property of the long run, not of any experience you'll have.

And the long run itself is shakier than it sounds: in 100 plays, there's a real chance — about 37% (0.99^100) — that the $1,000 ball never comes up at all, and you lose the entire $1,000. Expected value smooths over that risk; your wallet lives in it.

This is why expected value is the right tool for insurers and casinos, who play millions of times, and a treacherous one for a person playing once. For single decisions, ask about the distribution: what happens most often, and what's the worst case I can afford? The average is the answer to a question about a crowd of parallel yous — and you only get to be one of them.

My kid averaged my two classes' test scores to tell me the school average: Class X averaged 80, Class Y averaged 60, so he said the school averaged 70. Class X has 10 students, Class Y has 30. He's wrong, isn't he?

He is — he averaged the averages, which only works when the groups are the same size. Go back to the raw totals.

- Class X: 10 students averaging 80 → total points = 10 x 80 = 800.
- Class Y: 30 students averaging 60 → total points = 30 x 60 = 1,800.
- School total: 800 + 1,800 = 2,600 points across 40 students.
- True school average: 2,600 / 40 = 65.

His 70 treated the two classes as equals, but Class Y has three times the students, so its 60 pulls the combined average much harder. The correct method weights each average by its group size — which is just a shortcut for adding up all the individual scores.

This error is everywhere once you look: averaging state-level rates to get a national rate, averaging monthly percentages to get a yearly one, averaging the averages of two clinics with different patient counts. Any time someone hands you an average of averages, ask for the group sizes. If the sizes differ, the number is wrong by exactly the imbalance — here, a full 5 points of phantom achievement.
My kid's homework says ice cream sales and drowning deaths are strongly correlated, and asks if ice cream causes drowning. Obviously not — but what's the actual explanation, with numbers?

The hidden third factor is summer. Both lines are really tracking heat and swimming, not each other.

Make up a small town's year. In winter: 10,000 ice creams sold, 1 drowning. In summer: 100,000 ice creams sold, 10 drownings. Plot those and the correlation is beautiful — drownings rise in lockstep with ice cream.

Now count the exposure that matters. Suppose winter sees 20,000 swimming outings and summer sees 200,000. Drowning rate per outing: winter 1 / 20,000; summer 10 / 200,000 — the same rate. Nothing about the water got more dangerous, and nothing about ice cream did anything. Ten times as many people swam, so ten times as many drownings occurred, and ten times as many ice creams were sold to the crowds at the beach.

The structure to teach: A and B can march together because C is conducting both. Heat drives ice cream sales up and drives people into the water, where a fixed small risk per swim produces more total tragedies.

The homework's real lesson: a correlation is a clue, never a verdict. Before believing A causes B, ask what C could be conducting — and the seasons are the most tireless conductor in all of statistics.
A headline says "Coffee drinkers die younger, study finds." My grandfather drank coffee for 70 years, so I'm skeptical. How could a study get that result if coffee is harmless?

By letting a confounder — something tangled up with both coffee and death — do the damage. Historically the big one was smoking: smokers drank a lot of coffee. Build the trap with 200 people.

Smokers (100 people): 80 drink coffee, of whom 16 die in the study period (20%). 20 don't drink coffee, of whom 4 die (20%).
Non-smokers (100 people): 20 drink coffee, of whom 1 dies (5%). 80 don't, of whom 4 die (5%).

Within each group, coffee drinkers and non-drinkers die at identical rates — coffee does nothing.

Now pool everyone, the way the headline does. Coffee drinkers: 100 people, 17 deaths = 17%. Non-drinkers: 100 people, 8 deaths = 8%. "Coffee drinkers die at twice the rate!"

The pooled comparison isn't really coffee versus no coffee; it's "a group that is 80% smokers" versus "a group that is 20% smokers," wearing coffee as a label. Good studies handle this by adjusting for smoking — comparing within groups, as we just did. When a headline rests on an observational study, the question to ask is: what differs between the groups besides the thing being studied, and did they account for it? If the answer is silence, the correlation is a costume on a confounder.

I have chronic back pain. It flares terribly for a week, then eases. Twice now I've tried a new remedy right at the worst point, and both times I felt much better within days. My friend says that proves nothing. That feels unfair — I was there, I felt it.

Your experience is real; the conclusion doesn't follow, and the reason has a name: regression to the mean. Pain that fluctuates has peaks and valleys. When do you try a new remedy? At the peak — nobody experiments when things are tolerable.

Put numbers on a flare pattern. Say 20 people start a remedy when their pain is 9 out of 10, the worst week. Back pain flares subside on their own: suppose that over the next two weeks, half of them would ease to 5 and half to 7 with no treatment at all. Average afterwards: (10 x 5 + 10 x 7) / 20 = 6. Everyone improved — from 9 to 6 — and the remedy was present for all of it.

The improvement is genuine; the attribution is the problem. Starting anything at the worst moment guarantees that "after" looks better than "before," whether the thing works or not. Remedies, management consultants, football coaches hired mid-slump — all of them surf regression to the mean.

How could you actually learn whether your remedy works? Use it at random flare levels, not just peaks — or better, track your pain daily in a notebook for a few months, remedies noted, and see whether treated flares end faster than untreated ones. That diary, boring as it is, knows more than any single dramatic recovery — including yours. Your friend is right about the proof and wrong if he implies your relief wasn't real. Both things fit.
Last year's Rookie of the Year hit .340. This year he's hitting .295 and the radio guys say he's "in a sophomore slump" and "lost his swing." Is there a dumber explanation that's probably right?

Yes: last year's .340 was partly luck, and luck doesn't renew its contract.

Suppose his true ability is a .290 hitter. Over a 500-at-bat season, a .290 hitter expects 145 hits. Last year he got 170 hits — a .340 average. Those extra 25 hits are the season's fortune: balls that dropped between fielders, seeing-eye singles, a few generous scorer's calls. Hitting is a skill measured in hundreds of near-coin-flips, and even a fair coin runs hot for stretches.

This year he's at .295 — 148-ish hits per 500 at-bats, right on top of his true .290 talent. Nothing was lost. The "slump" is the difference between a lucky measurement and an honest one.

The pattern is general and ruthless: whoever tops a noisy ranking in one period — rookie, fund manager, sales rep, restaurant of the year — was probably good and lucky. Next period the skill remains and the luck re-rolls, so they slide toward their true level. Pundits then invent a story (lost swing, sophomore slump, complacency) to explain what randomness did for free.

Before accepting any narrative about decline, ask: decline from what baseline — the person's demonstrated long-run level, or their single best measurement? Most "slumps" are just a career average reasserting itself.

People keep telling me randomized controlled trials are the "gold standard" and observational studies are weak. But if a study follows 100,000 people for years, isn't that better than some trial with 2,000? What does randomization actually buy?

It buys the one thing size can't: groups that differ only by the treatment. Watch what goes wrong without it.

In an observational study of a vitamin, the people who take it chose to. They also tend to exercise more, smoke less, earn more, and see doctors sooner — the "healthy user" tangle. If vitamin-takers end up healthier, you cannot separate the vitamin's effect from the lifestyle that came bundled with it. Following 100,000 such people for a decade just measures the tangle very precisely. Big samples shrink random error; they do nothing at all to bias — they give you a very accurate answer to the wrong question.

Randomization breaks the tangle at the root. Take 2,000 people and flip a coin for each: pill or placebo. Now the exercisers, smokers, rich and poor land in both groups in roughly equal numbers — not by anyone's cleverness, but by the coin. Crucially, this includes confounders nobody has thought of yet. The only systematic difference left between the groups is the pill.

That's why a 2,000-person randomized trial can settle a question that a 100,000-person observational study merely argues about. Size fights variance; randomization fights confounding. They're different enemies, and only one of the two weapons works on each.

The honest caveat: trials have their own limits — they're short, they enroll selected people, and you can't randomize everything (nobody assigns smoking). But when a trial is possible, its small clean comparison outweighs a giant tangled one.
My daughter's science fair poster says "Kids with bigger feet read better — shoe size predicts reading level!" She's 8 and very proud. Is she wrong?

She's measured something real and concluded something false, which makes it a perfect science fair poster — the fix will teach her more than the project did.

Her data is probably genuine. Sample two classrooms:

- 6-year-olds: average shoe size around a child's 12, reading at about level 2.
- 10-year-olds: average shoe size around an adult 4, reading at about level 6.

Plot shoe size against reading level across both classes and the line climbs beautifully. But neither causes the other: age is conducting both. Feet grow because children get older; reading improves because children get older and get taught. Within a single classroom of same-aged kids, the correlation mostly evaporates — the big-footed 6-year-old reads like a 6-year-old.

The gentle way to show her: split her data by age and re-plot. If the pattern survives inside each age group, she's onto something; if it vanishes, age was doing all the work. That's the confounder test, and learning it at 8 puts her ahead of most headline writers.

Praise the measurement, question the arrow. "Predicts" is doing sneaky work in her title — shoe size predicts reading level the way a birthday predicts both, without causing either.
A city council member noticed that fires with more firefighters sent end up with more property damage, and suggested sending fewer trucks. Please explain, with numbers, why that's backwards.

The firefighters aren't causing the damage; the size of the fire is causing both. Two kinds of fires:

- 10 small fires (a bin, a stove): the dispatcher sends 1 truck; average damage $10,000.
- 10 large fires (a warehouse, a block): the dispatcher sends 5 trucks; average damage $500,000.

Now pool the data the council member's way: fires with 1 truck average $10,000 in damage; fires with 5 trucks average $500,000. "More firefighters, fifty times the damage!" The correlation is real, strong, and the causation runs the opposite way: damage potential summoned the trucks.

This is reverse causation tangled with a confounder (fire size drives both variables). Sending fewer trucks to a warehouse fire wouldn't make it a stove fire; it would make it a bigger warehouse fire.

The test that separates the stories: compare fires of the same size with different responses — or ask which came first and what decided it. Dispatchers send trucks because of the fire's scale; the arrow points from damage to firefighters, not back. Any time a response correlates with the severity of the problem — ambulances at fatal crashes, tutors for failing students, police at riots — expect this exact illusion, and expect someone to propose abolishing the response.

A study made headlines: "Moderate wine drinkers live longer than non-drinkers." My uncle, a lifelong non-drinker, is annoyed. A doctor on TV said the comparison group is "poisoned." What did she mean?

She meant the "non-drinkers" are secretly two different groups, and one of them is sick. Split them:

- Lifelong abstainers: 100 people, 12 die over the follow-up period (12%).
- Former drinkers — many of whom quit because of illness or a doctor's warning: 50 people, 15 die (30%).
- Moderate drinkers: 150 people, 15 die (10%).

Now pool the non-drinkers the way the headline does: 150 people, 27 deaths = 18%. Compare with the moderate drinkers' 10%, and wine looks like medicine.

But the honest comparison is lifelong abstainers versus moderate drinkers: 12% versus 10% — a small gap that other lifestyle differences could easily explain. The dramatic version exists only because the "non-drinker" bucket was stocked with people who stopped drinking precisely because their health was already failing. Researchers call this the sick-quitter effect.

The general lesson travels well: whenever a study compares groups, ask who exactly is in the comparison group and how they got there. "Non-users" of anything — a drug, a food, a technology — often include people who quit because it harmed them or because they got sick. That hidden composition can manufacture a benefit for the remaining users out of thin air.

I saw a chart showing that the number of Nicolas Cage movies per year correlates almost perfectly with people drowning in swimming pools. It's a famous example but nobody explained WHY such a match happens by chance.

Because with few data points and thousands of possible pairings, spectacular coincidences are guaranteed to exist somewhere — and someone goes looking for them.

The chart has about 10 yearly points. Any two wiggly lines over 10 points have a decent chance of wandering in the same general direction, especially if both happen to rise into a peak and fall off. Now multiply that opportunity: there are thousands of measurable yearly series — movie releases by actor, cheese consumption, bee colonies, arcade revenue — and millions of pairs you could plot against each other. If you test enough pairs, some pair will match at 99% correlation the way a lottery always has a winner: not because that ticket was special, but because so many tickets were sold.

Nobody plotted "Cage movies versus things that don't correlate" and published it. You only ever see the winning ticket.

The tell is the absence of a mechanism and the presence of a search. A correlation found by trawling thousands of series, with no story for how A could move B, is entertainment. A correlation predicted in advance from a theory, then confirmed in fresh data, is evidence. The chart can't tell you which kind you're looking at — the history of how it was found can.

Our company's worst store got a new manager and a consulting team in January. By March its sales jumped from 60% of target to 85%. The consultants are taking full credit in their pitch deck. Should they?

They should take some questions first. The store was selected for intervention because it was the worst — and "the worst right now" is usually a mixture of genuinely weak and temporarily unlucky.

Say the chain has 20 stores, all with a true level around 85% of target, wobbling month to month by luck: weather, roadworks, a competitor's promotion. In any given month, the unluckiest store might post 60% — not because it's the worst-run, but because the wobbles lined up against it. The roadworks end, the weather normalizes, and next quarter it posts 85% with no intervention at all. That's regression to the mean: extreme measurements are extreme partly by chance, and chance doesn't persist.

The consultants arrived exactly at the extreme — interventions are always scheduled at extremes, since nobody hires help for an average month — so the natural rebound was booked as their effect.

How would you ever know if they helped? Compare against similar struggling stores that didn't get consultants, or check whether the improvement exceeds the usual rebound of past worst-stores. If last year's worst store also bounced from the 60s to the 80s unaided, the deck is selling you the calendar. The improvement is real; the credit is unproven — and the difference between those two sentences is where consulting fees live.

A trial reports: "Patients improved 35% on the new pain drug." Buried in the paper, the placebo group improved 30%. The company says the drug works. My pharmacist says "barely." Who's framing it honestly?

Your pharmacist. Count 100 patients per group.

- Placebo: 30 of 100 improve.
- Drug: 35 of 100 improve.

The drug's own contribution is the difference: 5 extra improvements per 100 patients. The other 30 improvements in the drug group would have happened anyway — some from the natural course of the condition (pain flares subside), some from regression to the mean (people enroll in trials when symptoms are worst), some from the placebo effect proper: expecting treatment, being monitored, being cared for.

The company's "35% improved" quietly credits the drug with all 35. The honest sentence is "5 more patients in 100 improved than on placebo" — an NNT of 20, if you want it in those terms: treat 20 people for one extra success.

That doesn't automatically make the drug worthless; for severe pain, 5 in 100 can matter, and side effects and cost complete the picture. But every trial result should be read as a subtraction: treatment minus control. The control group is the price of honesty — it's the only thing standing between a real effect and the impressive-sounding background rate at which people simply get better.
There's a real published study correlating a country's chocolate consumption with its number of Nobel Prize winners. Switzerland tops both. Should I eat chocolate for my brain?

The correlation is real; the conclusion is a mirage, and the study's own author knew it — it was published partly as a provocation.

The conductor here is wealth. Rich countries can afford imported chocolate as a daily habit; rich countries also fund universities, laboratories, and the decades of research careers that Nobel Prizes crown. Line up countries by wealth and both lines climb together, without a single cocoa molecule touching a single neuron.
