Notice the unit trick, too: the correlation is between country averages. It says nothing about people. Within Switzerland, the laureates are not necessarily the champion chocolate eaters; country-level patterns routinely fail to describe individuals (the ecological fallacy).

And Switzerland is exactly the kind of point that inflates such correlations: a small, rich country, extreme on both measures, dragging the line toward itself.

Enjoy chocolate for the reasons chocolate is enjoyable. If it sharpened minds at population scale, the effect would have to survive comparisons within countries, across individuals, with wealth held constant — and nobody has shown that, because the chocolate was never the variable doing the work. The money was.

A study of hospitalized patients found that two unrelated conditions almost never occur together, and concluded one might protect against the other. A statistician friend muttered "Berkson" and shook his head. What's the problem?

The problem is that the study only looked inside a hospital — and being in the hospital is a consequence of having either condition, which warps everything. This is Berkson's paradox, a collider bias. Build it:

In a general population of 10,000, conditions A and B are independent, each affecting 100 people. Expected overlap by pure chance: 100 x 100 / 10,000 = 1 person with both. So: 99 have only A, 99 have only B, 1 has both, 9,801 have neither.

Now the hospital admits everyone with A or B, and almost nobody else. The ward holds 99 + 99 + 1 = 199 patients. Look at the ward's numbers:

- Among patients with A (100 of them), only 1 also has B: 1%.
- Among patients without A (99 of them), all 99 have B — that's why they're here: 100%.

Inside the hospital, A and B look violently opposed: having A seems to "protect" you from B. In the population, they're completely independent. Nothing biological happened; the sampling frame manufactured the association, because admission is a common effect — a collider — of the two conditions, and conditioning on it forces them to look negatively related.

Anywhere the data is "people who showed up" — hospital patients, clinic attendees, survey respondents, app users — ask whether showing up depends on the variables being studied. If it does, correlations inside the room can be artifacts of the door.
A report says "towns with more churches have more crime" and a talk-show host is having a field day. Demolish it with arithmetic, please.

Gladly. The missing variable is town size — more people means more of everything, including churches and crimes.

- Town A: population 1,000. Churches: 2. Crimes last year: 10.
- Town B: population 10,000. Churches: 20. Crimes last year: 100.

Town B has ten times the churches and ten times the crime — the correlation across towns is real. Now divide by population:

- Churches per person: A has 2 / 1,000 = 1 per 500 people. B has 20 / 10,000 = 1 per 500 people. Identical.
- Crime rate: A has 10 / 1,000 = 1 per 100 people. B has 100 / 10,000 = 1 per 100 people. Identical.

The towns are exactly alike in every way that matters; only their size differs, and raw counts scale with size. Comparing totals between places of different sizes almost always produces this phantom: more hospitals, more murders; more schools, more truancy; more ice cream shops, more drownings.

The fix is the rate: divide by population before comparing anything across places. It's the same move as per-capita income, and it's why demographers treat raw counts from unequal populations as unquotable. The talk-show version survives because "per 100 residents, the towns are identical" has never once been a good segment.
One channel says unemployment "rose 25%," another says it "rose 1 point," about the same jobs report. Unemployment went from 4% to 5%. Which channel is lying?

Neither — they're reporting the same change with different rulers, and each chose the ruler that fits its story.

The change in the rate itself: 5% - 4% = 1 percentage point. That's the "rose 1 point" version.

The change relative to where it started: 1 / 4 = 25%. That's the "rose 25%" version.

Put workers on it: in a labor force of 1,000, unemployment going from 4% to 5% means jobless people rise from 40 to 50. Ten more people out of work per thousand. One channel makes that sound like a tremor; the other makes it sound like a quake.

When the quantity is itself a percentage, always ask: points or percent? Percentage points are the subtraction; percent change is the subtraction divided by the starting value. Confusing them inflates or deflates any rate change by design. Interest rates, tax rates, poll numbers, unemployment — the two versions will always both be available, and someone will pick the one that serves the headline.
Our big city reported 1,200 burglaries last year. A small town nearby reported only 60, and its mayor calls it "20 times safer." The city has 1,000,000 people; the town has 20,000. Check the mayor.

The mayor is comparing counts between places of wildly different sizes. Convert both to rates per 100,000 residents — the standard unit.

- City: 1,200 / 1,000,000 = 0.0012, which is 120 burglaries per 100,000 people.
- Town: 60 / 20,000 = 0.003, which is 300 burglaries per 100,000 people.

Per resident, the town's burglary rate is 300 / 120 = 2.5 times the city's. The town isn't 20 times safer; by rate, it's two and a half times more burgled. The mayor's "20 times" came from 1,200 / 60 — a ratio of raw counts that mostly measures the fact that the city has 50 times the people.

This is the single most common statistical error in local news: ranking places by counts. Any total — crimes, accidents, disease cases — scales with population, so big places always look dangerous and small places always look calm until you divide.

The habit to build: whenever you see a count attached to a place, ask "out of how many people?" and convert to a rate before feeling anything about it.

A village of 200 people had zero murders for a decade, then one this year. A website ranked it "the most dangerous village in the country" with a murder rate of 500 per 100,000. Is the ranking just wrong, or is something deeper going on?

The arithmetic is right and the ranking is meaningless — rates from tiny denominators are unstable to the point of comedy.

The village's rate: 1 murder / 200 people = 0.005, which scaled per 100,000 is indeed 500. Last year the same calculation gave 0 per 100,000 — the "safest village in the country." One event swung the village from best to worst in the nation, because each single case is worth 500 points of rate.

Compare a city of 1,000,000 with 500 murders: its rate is 500 / 1,000,000 = 50 per 100,000, and it would take 5,000 murders — ten times as many — to print the village's headline number. The city's rate barely moves when one more crime occurs (each case is worth 0.1 points); the village's explodes.

Statisticians handle this by demanding a minimum denominator, averaging over multiple years, or shrinking small-sample rates toward the overall average. The deeper principle: a rate is an estimate, and its reliability lives in the denominator. 1-out-of-200 and 5,000-out-of-1,000,000 can print similar-looking rates with utterly different trustworthiness.

Whenever a ranking involves small places, small schools, small hospitals — check the denominators before the drama. The extremes of any league table are usually occupied by the smallest units, at both ends, for purely mathematical reasons.

Reported assaults in our city jumped 40% in the year after the police launched an easy reporting app. The mayor's opponent says the city is collapsing. The police chief says nothing changed but paperwork. Who's more likely right?

The chief has the stronger story, and here's the arithmetic that supports it.

Suppose the city always had about 1,000 actual assaults a year, but historically only half were ever reported: 500 reports.

After the app launches, reporting gets easier — victims who wouldn't visit a station now file from their phones. Say the reporting rate rises to 70%: 0.70 x 1,000 = 700 reports.

Reports went from 500 to 700: that's exactly a 40% increase (200 / 500), with the true number of assaults completely unchanged at 1,000. The entire "surge" is the measurement improving.

How would you check? Look for a measure that doesn't depend on reporting: victimization surveys (which ask a random sample of residents directly) or hospital admissions for assault injuries. If those are flat while reports climb, the city isn't more violent — it's better counted. This pattern is so common it has a rhythm: a new hotline, app, or awareness campaign launches, reports spike, and the spike is evidence the channel works, not that the problem exploded.

Recorded crime is a count of reports passing through a system. Whenever the system changes — new app, new definition, new recording rules — the series breaks, and year-on-year comparisons across the break are meaningless until someone shows you an independent measure.
A jacket was $100, went up 50%, then went on sale at "50% off." My brother says it's free money — back to $100. I paid $75. Explain to my brother.

Your receipt is right, and the reason is that the two 50%s are taken from different amounts.

- Start: $100.
- Up 50%: 50% of $100 is $50, so the price becomes $150.
- Down 50%: 50% of $150 is $75, so the price becomes $150 - $75 = $75.

The increase added $50; the decrease removed $75. Percentages are always "of" something, and the second percentage was of a bigger something.

The general rule: a rise of X% followed by a fall of X% never cancels — you always end below where you started (for increases-then-decreases on the same quantity), because the fall acts on the inflated value. To undo a 50% rise exactly, you'd need a fall of 33.3%: $50 off $150.

This asymmetry runs markets and headlines: a stock that falls 50% needs a 100% gain just to break even. When someone chains percentages together for you, convert each step to actual amounts — the dollars never lie about which base was used.

A health alert says a contaminant was found in "0.02% of tested wells" in our county, and separately that there were "20 cases per 100,000 residents" of some illness. My neighbor treats these as totally different scales. Are they?

They're the same scale wearing two outfits. Convert:

20 per 100,000 = 20 / 100,000 = 0.0002 = 0.02%. Identical quantity.

Per-100,000 and percent are just different magnifications. Percent zooms to hundredths (per 100); per-100,000 zooms a thousand times further, which is why public health uses it for rare things — "0.02%" is hard to feel, "20 per 100,000" at least has whole people in it.

To make it concrete for your county: if it has 250,000 residents, a rate of 20 per 100,000 means 2.5 x 20 = 50 actual cases. That's the move that matters: rate → your population → expected count.

Writers pick the unit that serves the story. Percent makes rare things look vanishing ("only 0.02%!"); raw counts make them look alarming ("50 residents affected!"). Both are honest; neither is complete. Fluency is converting between them on sight: percent = per-100,000 divided by 1,000; per-100,000 = percent times 1,000.
The store offered "20% off, plus an extra 20% off at the register." I expected 40% off my $100 shoes and paid $64. Did they cheat me?

No — successive percentages multiply rather than add, because the second discount applies to the already-discounted price.

- Start: $100.
- First 20% off: $100 - $20 = $80.
- Extra 20% off: 20% of $80 is $16, so $80 - $16 = $64.

Total discount: $36 off $100 = 36%, not 40%. The missing 4% is the discount on the discount: you don't get 20% off the $20 you already saved.

The general pattern: two 20% cuts compound to 0.8 x 0.8 = 0.64 of the price remaining. Any chain of percentage changes works this way — multiply the survival factors (1 - 0.20) rather than adding the percentages. Three stacked 20% discounts would be 0.8 x 0.8 x 0.8 = 0.512, a 48.8% total cut, still not 60%.

Retailers know shoppers add percentages in their heads, which is exactly why the offer is phrased as two twenties instead of one honest 36. When discounts stack, multiply; when a single number would be less exciting, expect it to arrive as a stack.

Two headlines from the same town data: "Traffic accidents UP 60% under the new mayor!" and "Roads safer than ever: accident rate DOWN 20%." The town's population grew from 10,000 to 20,000, and accidents went from 50 to 80. Both headlines are from real numbers?

Both are real; they're measuring different things, and the population growth is what lets them diverge.

Counts: accidents rose from 50 to 80. Increase: 30 / 50 = 60%. Headline one checks out.

Rates: divide by population.

- Before: 50 / 10,000 = 500 accidents per 100,000 residents.
- After: 80 / 20,000 = 400 per 100,000 residents.
- Change: 400 vs 500 is a 20% decrease. Headline two checks out.

For any individual resident, the risk of being in an accident fell by a fifth — that's the rate, and it's usually the number that describes lived experience. The total count rose because there are twice as many people to have accidents. A growing town will set "record" totals for almost everything — accidents, crimes, weddings, library books — every year, automatically.

When a place is changing size, counts answer "how much work does the system handle?" (useful for budgeting ambulances) and rates answer "how risky is it to live here?" (useful for judging safety). Politicians will pick whichever flatters them. Your job is to notice which question you actually care about and demand that number.
An ad brags "sales increased 300%!" — from 10 units a day to... I say 40, my friend says 30. Who's right, and why is everyone confused by this?

You're right: 40. An increase of 300% means the increase itself equals 300% of the original.

- Original: 10 units.
- Increase: 300% of 10 = 30 units.
- New total: 10 + 30 = 40 units.

Your friend computed 300% of 10 = 30 and stopped — that's "sales rose to 300% of what they were," which is a different claim (and only a 200% increase: going from 10 to 30 adds 20, which is 200% of 10).

The confusion is built into the language: "increased BY 300%" (add three times the original → 4x total) versus "increased TO 300%" (end at three times the original → 3x total). One word flips the answer. Advertisers exploit the fog by choosing whichever phrasing the audience will misread upward.

The safe habit: never convert a percent increase into a multiplier in your head. Ask for the two counts — from how many, to how many — and compute the change yourself: (new - old) / old. For 10 → 40: (40 - 10) / 10 = 300%. For 10 → 30: 200%. The counts can't be spun; the percent phrasing can.
A toothpaste ad says "50% fewer cavities!" The study behind it: kids using regular toothpaste averaged 2.0 cavities a year, kids using this one averaged 1.0. My dentist shrugged at the ad. Why?

Because the relative number and the lived number are telling different stories, and your dentist works in the lived one.

The relative claim: (2.0 - 1.0) / 2.0 = 50% fewer cavities. True.

The absolute claim: one fewer cavity per child per year. Also true — and for an individual parent deciding whether the premium price is worth it, that's the operative fact: over a childhood of, say, 10 years of brushing, about 10 fewer cavities, assuming the effect holds.

Whether that's impressive depends on the baseline, which the ad never mentions. "50% fewer" built on a baseline of 2 is one cavity; the same slogan built on a baseline of 0.02 cavities (2 per 100 kids) would mean one cavity prevented per 100 child-years — and the ad would look identical.

Your dentist's shrug is the professional version of the base-rate question: reductions are always relative to something, and the something decides whether the claim is a breakthrough or a rounding error. "50% fewer" is the shape of the effect. "From 2 to 1 per year" is its size. Buy sizes, not shapes.
Town A's overall death rate is 0.59% a year. Retirement Town B's is 4.51% — nearly eight times higher! A coworker says B must have terrible healthcare. I suspect the towns' age mixes. Who's right?

You are, and the proof is that both towns have identical death rates at every age. Give each town 10,000 residents and the same age-specific rates: young people die at 0.1% a year, old people at 5% a year.

Town A (young town): 9,000 young, 1,000 old.
- Young deaths: 0.1% x 9,000 = 9.
- Old deaths: 5% x 1,000 = 50.
- Total: 59 deaths / 10,000 = 0.59%.

Town B (retirement town): 1,000 young, 9,000 old.
- Young deaths: 0.1% x 1,000 = 1.
- Old deaths: 5% x 9,000 = 450.
- Total: 451 / 10,000 = 4.51%.

Same medical reality, wildly different headline rates — the entire gap is the age mix. B doesn't have worse outcomes; it has older residents, and old residents die at higher rates everywhere on Earth.

This is why demographers age-adjust rates before comparing places: they recompute each town's rate as if it had a standard population's age mix, which strips out exactly this illusion. Any crude comparison of death rates, disease rates, or even average incomes between populations with different age structures is suspect until adjusted. Your coworker compared two pyramids and blamed the doctors.
An ad claims a supplement "reduces your risk of deficiency by 150%." My brother says that's impossible. Is he right, or is this some technical usage?

Your brother is right, and it's worth seeing why, because the impossibility is a useful detector.

A reduction is measured against the starting amount, and you can't reduce something by more than all of it. If your risk is 10%, the largest possible reduction is 10 percentage points — a 100% reduction, bringing you to zero. A "150% reduction" would put your risk at 10% - 15% = -5%, and negative risk doesn't exist.

What might the advertiser have meant? Possibly that a dose or blood level increased by 150% (increases can exceed 100% freely: from 10 to 25 is a 150% increase). Or that the supplement is "2.5 times as effective" at something. Or nothing at all — the number may simply be engineered to sound big, counting on readers not to check it against the ceiling.

Either way, a reduction claim over 100% tells you the copy wasn't written by anyone respecting the arithmetic, which is itself information about the product. File it with its cousins: "150% more efficient," "300% less fat." Decreases cap at 100%; increases don't. Any claim that breaks the cap is broken, full stop.
A study of 12 people found a supplement "significantly improved memory scores." The product's website is very excited. Should I be?

Let the size of the study set your excitement level. Twelve people is not a sample; it's a dinner party.

Each person is 1/12 — over 8% — of the entire dataset. If one participant slept well before the retest, or happened to get an easier word list, that single person's good day moves the group average by a visible amount. In a study of 1,200, one person's good day is 0.08% of the data and vanishes. In a study of 12, individual luck is a load-bearing wall.

Small studies also suffer a selection effect: with tiny samples, only implausibly large effects can cross the "significance" line, so the small studies that do get published tend to report inflated effects that shrink when anyone repeats them with more people — the winner's curse.

None of this proves the supplement does nothing. It proves this study can't tell. File it as "interesting if replicated," and check whether the website mentions any larger follow-up. A result that only exists at n = 12 exists mostly as marketing material.
I'm reading a trial of a blood pressure drug for my dad. The results look great — but the "exclusion criteria" section is long. Why should I care who was kept out of a study?

Because the drug was only proven on the people who were let in, and the exclusions describe exactly whose results you're not seeing.

Read the list as a portrait of the studied patient. A typical trial might enroll 2,000 people but exclude: anyone over 75, anyone with kidney disease, anyone with diabetes, anyone taking more than two other medications. Each exclusion makes the trial cleaner — fewer complications, clearer signal — and less like the real clinic.

Now hold your dad up against the portrait. If he's 78 with diabetes and a kidney issue, he is three-for-three on the excluded list. The trial's tidy result — say blood pressure down 12 points with few side effects — was measured on people systematically healthier than him. In his body, the benefit could be smaller and the side effects (which often appear precisely in kidneys, in the elderly, in people on multiple drugs) larger, and the trial contains no information either way, because people like him were never in it.

This isn't fraud; it's a boundary. Every study result comes with an invisible label: "demonstrated in people who look like this." Before applying any result to a real person, compare that person to the inclusion portrait. The further they are from it, the more the result is a hope rather than a finding.

A cholesterol drug trial was designed to study heart attacks, but the published paper mostly celebrates that cholesterol dropped 30%. A critic called this "moving the goalposts." Explain what's fishy.

The fishy part is the swap of endpoints — the outcome the trial promised to measure versus the outcome it reported.

The trial's registration said the primary endpoint was heart attacks: the event patients actually care about. Cholesterol is a surrogate endpoint — a lab number believed to predict heart attacks. When the paper leads with "cholesterol down 30%," the natural question is what happened to the heart attacks, and the answer is usually that the difference was small or absent, which is why it isn't in the headline.

Why it matters: surrogates can mislead. A drug can move a lab value beautifully while the real outcome doesn't follow — the body is not a spreadsheet, and a marker is a hypothesis about the disease, not the disease. History has examples in both directions, which is exactly why trials pre-register a primary endpoint: to stop researchers from shopping among outcomes after the fact and reporting whichever moved.

So the reading habit: find the primary endpoint (it's in the trial registry and usually the methods section), and judge the paper on that. If the celebrated result is a different, softer outcome than the promised one, treat the paper as an advertisement for a result it didn't get. A 30% cholesterol drop is a fact about blood chemistry. Whether anyone had fewer heart attacks is the question the trial was built to answer — insist on hearing it answered.
A study comparing two painkillers was funded by the maker of one of them, and — surprise — their drug won, 70% relief versus 55%. Does the funding mean I should just dismiss it?

Dismissing it outright would be as lazy as trusting it outright. Funding is a reason to inspect the design, not a verdict — and in this case the design is where the fingerprints usually are.

Ask how the comparison was dosed. A classic maneuver: the sponsor's drug at its full recommended dose against the competitor at half dose. Pain relief 70% versus 55% then measures dosing generosity, not drug quality. Other quiet levers: choosing the time point where your drug peaks, enrolling patients who previously responded well to your drug's class, or setting the competitor's dose schedule awkwardly.

Here's the useful frame: funding tells you who had a motive; the methods section tells you whether they had the opportunity. A funded study with a fair design — matched doses, pre-registered endpoint, independent analysis — can be perfectly good evidence. An independently funded study with a rigged design is still rigged.

So read it in this order: endpoint, doses, who was enrolled, who analyzed the data. If those are clean, the funding is a footnote. If the doses are lopsided, you don't need to know who paid — the comparison was never a contest. Your skepticism is healthy; aim it at the design, where it can actually land.
There's a famous story that a study found "green jelly beans cause acne" with p < 0.05. It was a joke about something real. What actually goes wrong when researchers test lots of things?

What goes wrong is that the 5% in "p < 0.05" is a false-alarm rate, and it applies per test. Test enough things and the alarms are guaranteed to ring.

In the jelly bean story, researchers test 20 colors, each against acne, at the standard threshold. For any one color with truly no effect, there's a 5% chance — 1 in 20 — of a fluke "significant" result. Run 20 tests and the expected number of flukes is 20 x 0.05 = 1. So one color — green, say — comes up p = 0.03 by pure chance, and that's the one that gets reported: "Green jelly beans linked to acne, study finds." The 19 null results go in a drawer.

Nothing was faked. Every step was standard; the error is in the accounting. The p-value answers "how surprising is this if nothing is going on — for this one test?" It silently assumes this test was the only one you ran, or the only one you cared about.

The defenses are simple to state: decide the hypothesis before looking (pre-registration), correct for multiple tests, or replicate the fluke in fresh data before believing it. And as a reader: when a finding is oddly specific — one color, one subgroup, one outcome among many — ask how many siblings it had. A lone significant result among twenty tries is the expected harvest of pure noise.
If a supplement does nothing, wouldn't the scientific literature eventually show that? A friend said the literature itself is biased even if every published study is honest. How?

Through the file drawer: studies that find nothing tend not to be published, so the literature is a filtered sample of the research actually done.

Imagine 10 labs test the same dud supplement.

- 9 labs find no effect. Journals aren't interested ("nothing happened" is a hard sell), the researchers move on, and those results sit in drawers.
- 1 lab, by luck, gets a fluke positive — with a 5% false-alarm rate per study and enough labs trying, flukes are expected — and publishes: "Supplement shows promise!"

Now search the literature: you find 1 study, and it's positive. The published record reads "1 out of 1 studies found an effect," while the true record is 1 out of 10. Every published study was honestly conducted and honestly reported; the bias is in which studies became visible at all.

This is publication bias, and it's why "studies show..." is weaker than it sounds for any claim where many groups might have quietly tried and failed. The countermeasures exist — trial registries that log studies before they run, journals that accept null results — and a careful reader gives extra weight to claims backed by registered trials and meta-analyses that hunt for unpublished data. A literature can be 100% honest and still lie by omission.

An abstract concludes a treatment "reduced the risk of complications by 33%" and never gives absolute numbers anywhere in the abstract. I have the full paper. Where do I find the real story, and what might it be?

Go to the results table and find the two raw counts: how many people in each group, and how many had the complication in each group. Everything honest can be rebuilt from those four numbers. Here's the kind of thing you often find:

- Control group: 3 complications per 1,000 patients (0.3%).
- Treatment group: 2 complications per 1,000 patients (0.2%).

Relative reduction: (3 - 2) / 3 = 33%. The abstract's claim, exactly.
Absolute reduction: 1 complication prevented per 1,000 patients treated — a number needed to treat of 1,000.

Both statements are the same data. The abstract chose the one that sounds like a breakthrough; the table contains the one that sounds like a rounding error. Which framing governs your decision depends on the treatment's cost, burden, and side effects weighed against 1-in-1,000 — a weighing the abstract has made impossible by hiding the denominator.

Make it a reflex: a relative effect with no absolute numbers is a claim with the price tag removed. Abstracts are advertisements for the paper; the table is the paper. If a journal or press release gives you only the percentage, assume the absolute number is unflattering until you've seen it — that assumption is right often enough to be a rule.

A huge trial — 100,000 people — found a headache pill "significantly shortened headaches, p < 0.001." The actual effect: headaches lasted 4 minutes less on average. How can something be that significant and that trivial?

Because "significant" answers a different question than "important." Statistical significance asks: could this difference be a mirage of random chance? Effect size asks: how big is it?

With 100,000 people, the noise averages out so thoroughly that even a whisper of a real effect becomes detectable. A 4-minute difference measured that precisely is almost certainly real — p < 0.001 says the odds of seeing this pattern by pure luck are under 1 in 1,000. It's a real 4 minutes.

But real and worthwhile are separate judgments. Four minutes off a headache is below most people's threshold of caring, no matter how certain it is. Contrast a small trial of 60 people finding a 90-minute reduction at p = 0.04: less certain, but if true, far more valuable.

The confusion is baked into the word: in everyday English "significant" means "matters"; in statistics it means "detectable." Papers exploit the double meaning constantly, especially in press releases. Train yourself to translate on sight: significant = "probably not zero." Then immediately ask the second question the headline skipped: "and how far from zero?" A result needs both a small p-value and a meaningful size before it deserves your attention.
A study's main result was negative — the treatment didn't work. But the press release trumpets that it "worked in left-handed women over 60." Should anyone believe that?

Almost certainly not, and the arithmetic of subgroups shows why. After a null main result, researchers can slice the data many ways: by age bands, sex, handedness, site, severity — say they examine 20 subgroups.

Each subgroup test at the usual threshold carries about a 5% false-alarm rate. Expected flukes: 20 x 0.05 = 1. So among 20 slices of a treatment that does nothing, one slice will typically light up as "significant" by pure chance. "Left-handed women over 60" — a group that might contain only 37 people in the whole trial — is exactly the shape of that fluke: tiny, specific, and discovered after the fact rather than predicted before it.

The tell is the order of operations. A subgroup effect named in advance ("we predict it works in older patients, because...") and then confirmed is evidence. A subgroup found by trawling after the main result failed is a lottery winner being interviewed about their system.

The legitimate use of the finding is as a hypothesis: it justifies a new trial enrolling left-handed women over 60 to test the claim cleanly. Until that trial exists, treat the press release as what it is — a negative study wearing a costume it found in the data.
A drug my doctor wants me on for life was tested in a 6-week trial with 500 people, and "no serious side effects were observed." How much reassurance is that, really?

Less than it sounds, because the trial's total exposure is tiny compared to a lifetime of use. Convert the trial into person-years — the unit that matters for harms that accumulate or arrive late.

500 people x 6 weeks = 3,000 person-weeks of exposure. Divide by 52: about 58 person-years.

Now suppose the drug causes a serious side effect in 1 person per 1,000 per year of use — rare enough to sound negligible. Expected cases in the trial: 58 x (1/1,000) = 0.058. The trial would see zero cases about 94% of the time — "none observed" is exactly what you'd expect even if the harm is real. The study was never capable of seeing it.

Scale the harm to your life instead: taken for 30 years, a 1-in-1,000-per-year risk compounds to roughly 3% over the prescription's life (about 30 x 0.1%, slightly less with compounding) — no longer negligible, and completely invisible to a 6-week trial.

This is why drugs are monitored after approval, and why "no serious side effects were observed" should always be followed by "in how many people, for how long?" Short trials can prove a drug works and catch common, immediate harms. Rare and slow harms are structurally beyond their reach — the reassurance they offer has an expiration date printed in person-years.
A university press release announces a "breakthrough Alzheimer's treatment." I found the actual paper: it's about 18 mice. Walk me through how the claim mutated on its way to the headline.

Each step in the chain quietly upgraded the claim. Follow it:

The paper: 18 mice bred to develop Alzheimer's-like symptoms. The treated group navigated a maze in 34 seconds versus 40 seconds for controls — about 15% faster — and a brain biomarker moved in the right direction. That's the entire finding: in 18 mice, a proxy measure of memory improved modestly.

The mutations from paper to headline:

- Mice became patients. Mouse models of Alzheimer's have predicted human success many times and delivered it rarely; most treatments that help these mice fail in people.
- A biomarker and 6 seconds became "memory." Maze time is a stand-in for cognition, not cognition itself — and the paper measured no human-relevant outcome at all.
- "Improved a measure by 15%" became "breakthrough," a word with no statistical content whatsoever.
- One lab, one experiment, 18 animals became a finding, skipping the replication that separates results from flukes — and with 18 mice, each animal is 5.6% of the data, so a couple of good maze-runners can carry the result.

None of the steps required lying; each retelling just rounded up. Press offices are paid to round up, and by the third retelling the rounding compounds into fiction. The antidote is to read one level down: find the paper's abstract and check the species, the sample size, and the actual endpoint. Thirty seconds of that will deflate most breakthroughs you ever meet.
A fund's marketing chart shows its value up 80%. A rival chart of the same fund shows it up only 20%. A third shows 44%. All three use real prices. How?

They chose different starting lines, and a percentage gain is meaningless until you know where the ruler's zero sits. Say the fund's price history is:

- Start of 2019: 100.
- January 2020 (a peak): 120.
- March 2020 (a crash bottom): 80.
- Today: 144.

Now compute the gain from each start:

- From the crash bottom: (144 - 80) / 80 = 80%. The marketer's chart.
- From the January peak: (144 - 120) / 120 = 20%. The rival's chart.
- From 2019: (144 - 100) / 100 = 44%. The boring third chart.

Same fund, same prices, three true statements. The starting date does all the persuasive work: beginning a chart at a bottom is the oldest cosmetic in finance, and the mirror-image trick (starting at a peak) is how critics make the same fund look stagnant.

The defense is to standardize your own ruler: always ask for returns over fixed, boring windows — 1, 5, and 10 years — and compare every fund on the same windows. A chart whose start date looks chosen (especially one beginning right after a famous crash) is a chart that was designed, and not for your benefit.
Every year some magazine profiles investors who "beat the market five years in a row," implying genius. A skeptic told me pure luck manufactures these people on schedule. Show me.

Imagine 1,000 investors whose stock picks are literally coin flips — each year, each has a 50% chance of beating the market by luck alone.

- After 1 year: about 500 have a perfect record.
- After 2 years: about 250.
- After 3 years: about 125.
- After 4 years: about 62.
- After 5 years: about 31.

Each year halves the pool: 1,000 / 2^5 = about 31 investors with flawless five-year records, produced by a process with zero skill in it. Those 31 are the ones magazines profile — and they look exactly like geniuses, complete with confident philosophies they'll happily explain.

The sleight is the invisible denominator. You never meet the 969 whose luck ran out in year two; they don't get profiles. Judging the 31 survivors without the 1,000 starters is survivorship bias in its purest form.

The test that separates luck from skill isn't a streak — it's what happens next, and whether the record survives fees, taxes, and a full market cycle. A five-year streak drawn from a big enough crowd is the expected output of randomness. Before admiring any streak, ask how large the starting crowd was: streaks are manufactured by the thousand, and only the winners are visible.
I caught myself feeling like everyone on social media has a more exciting life than me. Intellectually I know it's a highlight reel. Can you make that concrete with numbers?

Count what your feed actually samples. Say you follow 100 friends, and each of them posts roughly their single best day each month — the trip, the promotion, the perfect dinner.

Your feed therefore shows you about 100 best-days per month. Each of those is the top 1 day out of that friend's 30 — the top 3% of their life, selected.

Your own month, which you experience unedited, contains 1 best day and 29 ordinary ones. So your brain compares your 100% sample (every day, including the dull and the bad) against their 3% sample (only the peaks), and concludes your life is below average. The comparison is rigged by sampling, not by anyone's actual happiness.

Notice nobody is lying. Each friend's post is real; the distortion is in the aggregation — a feed is a machine for concentrating peaks. The same machine runs in business ("every startup I read about is crushing it") and in science publishing ("every result I see is positive"): wherever only the highlights get transmitted, the transmitted world looks impossibly good.

The correction isn't to quit the feed; it's to fix the denominator in your head. Those 100 peak days came from 3,000 total days of other people's months — 2,900 of which were as ordinary as yours. You're not behind. You're unfiltered.
I've been to the gym 5 times in the last two weeks and announced to my wife that I'm "a consistent gym person now." She was... skeptical. What would a statistician say?

The statistician would ask about your base rate — the sample that matters isn't the last 14 days, it's your history. And the last two weeks are a tiny, self-selected sample: people start tracking and announcing precisely when motivation spikes, so the measurement window is chosen at the peak, like timing a remedy at the worst of a flare.

Put it in counts. Suppose last January you also went 12 times in the first two weeks, then 6 times in February, then stopped by March — a common pattern. Your lifetime gym data might be: 200 planned weeks, about 15 attended. Your personal base rate for "will I still be going in three months" is written in that history, and it doesn't care how sincere this January feels.

Two weeks of data also can't distinguish a new habit from a good fortnight: 5 visits is consistent with both. The honest test is boring and pre-committed: pick a window in advance — say, the next 12 weeks — and a threshold, like 24 visits, and judge only when the window closes. No renegotiating at week 3.

Your wife isn't doubting your effort; she's consulting your track record, which is the correct dataset. The encouraging flip side: base rates describe the past, and the way to beat yours is to survive the window where the old pattern used to quit. Check back in 12 weeks — with the notebook, not the feeling.

I play poker with friends monthly and I'd swear I "usually come out ahead." My buddy who keeps a spreadsheet says over our last 20 games I won 6, lost 14, and I'm down $340 total. How can my memory be that wrong?

Your memory isn't broken; it's a biased sample, and it's biased in a specific direction. Wins are vivid — the big pot, the bluff that worked — and get rehearsed in stories. Losses are dull and get filed under "cards were cold," a category your brain treats as weather rather than data.

The spreadsheet counts what memory filters. 20 sessions: 6 wins is a 30% win rate — you come out ahead less than a third of the time, the opposite of "usually." And the money agrees: -$340 over 20 games is -$17 per game on average, a slow leak that no individual night felt like, because the 6 wins were chunky and memorable while the 14 losses were mostly small and forgettable.

This is the universal pattern behind "my system works," "this remedy helps me," "I always pick the fast lane": impressions are compiled from the memorable cases, and memorability correlates with exactly the outcomes you're trying to count fairly. The lane you picked feels faster because you remember passing people, not the times you crawled.

The fix is always the same and always unglamorous: write it down at the time, every time, wins and losses alike. A contemporaneous log is the only version of the past that isn't campaigning for a conclusion. Your buddy's spreadsheet isn't smarter than your memory — it's just not allowed to forget on purpose.

Whenever my insomnia gets unbearable — five bad nights in a row — I try some new sleep remedy, and it always seems to work for a while. My doctor gently suggested the remedies might be getting credit for something else. What?

For the calendar. Insomnia that comes in waves has peaks, and you intervene at the peak by definition — nobody researches remedies after a decent night. But a five-bad-night streak is an extreme, and extremes end on their own.

Think of your sleep as fluctuating around your personal average, with good and bad stretches arriving in clumps. A run of five terrible nights is the far tail of that fluctuation. What follows a tail, with or without any remedy, is almost always something closer to your average — the streak breaks because streaks break. You then observe: took remedy, slept better. The remedy was present for a recovery that was already scheduled.

It's regression to the mean wearing pajamas, and the timing rule — "I try things when it's worst" — guarantees the illusion can never fail. Every remedy you test this way will "work," which is why you've accumulated several that seem to.

How to test one fairly: decide in advance to use it on a schedule rather than at peaks — alternate weeks, say — and keep a simple sleep diary for two months. Then compare average sleep in remedy weeks versus non-remedy weeks, including the weeks that weren't desperate. If the remedy earns its keep, it will show up there. If it only ever "works" when started at rock bottom, the diary will show the rock bottoms recovering on their own in the off weeks too.
I've read ten profiles of successful founders and almost all of them swear by waking at 5 a.m. I'm setting my alarm. Before I do — is the evidence actually any good?

The profiles commit a sampling error: they only interview winners, so they can't tell you whether the habit separates winners from losers. Build the full table with plausible numbers.

Imagine 10,000 founders, of whom 100 succeed (1%).

- Of the 100 successes, 80 wake at 5 a.m. — that's your ten profiles: early rising looks universal among winners (80%).
- Of the 9,900 failures, suppose 7,000 also woke at 5 a.m. (about 71%) — failures just don't get profiled.

Now compute what the alarm actually buys: among all 5 a.m. risers (80 + 7,000 = 7,080 people), the success rate is 80 / 7,080 ≈ 1.1%. Among everyone else it's 20 / 2,920 ≈ 0.7%. The base rate was 1%. Waking early moves you from 1% to about 1.1% — a rounding error dressed as a secret.

The profiles weren't lying; 80% of winners really do the habit. But a habit shared by 71% of losers can't explain winning. To evaluate any "habits of successful people" claim, you need the habit's frequency among the unsuccessful — the group books never profile.

Set the alarm if mornings suit you. Just don't mistake a near-universal habit for a cause: it's the founder equivalent of noting that 100% of winners drank water.
I keep hearing about bad reactions to a vaccine — a coworker, and someone in my running club. Two people! My sister says I should ask "out of how many?" Why is that the right question?

Because your brain counts cases, and cases without a denominator are meaningless. "Two people I know had a bad reaction" becomes information only when you know how many vaccinated people you know in total.

Say you know about 200 vaccinated people — coworkers, club members, family, friends. Two notable reactions among them is 2 / 200 = 1%. And even that overstates what you can conclude, because of how the sample reached you: reactions get mentioned; non-reactions don't. Nobody posts "got my shot Tuesday, felt nothing, carried on." The 198 uneventful vaccinations are invisible precisely because nothing happened — your information stream is filtered for events.

This is denominator neglect, and it's why anecdotes feel so much stronger than statistics: two vivid stories outweigh a silent 198 in your head, when arithmetically the 198 are the story.

Your sister's question is the universal solvent. Two reactions out of 200 acquaintances is a 1% rate worth comparing against official figures. Two out of 3 people you know would be alarming. Two out of 2,000,000 doses nationally would be astonishingly safe. The numerator never changes — the denominator is where the meaning lives.

I track about 15 health metrics on my watch. Every month I review them, and there's always one that improved a lot — which I credit to whatever I changed that month (new diet tweak, new supplement). My partner says I'm fooling myself. Is there math behind her rudeness?

There is, and it's the multiple-comparisons trap turned inward. Each of your 15 metrics wobbles month to month from pure noise — sleep, stress, measurement error — even when nothing about you changes. Suppose each metric has about a 1-in-20 chance in any month of jumping by an amount that looks impressive, just by luck.

Expected impressive jumps per month from noise alone: 15 x (1/20) = 0.75. So in most months, roughly one metric will stage a dramatic improvement for no reason — and that's before counting that you also glance at declines less eagerly. You then attach the month's change (the supplement, the diet tweak) to whichever metric jumped. The explanation is written after seeing which horse won.

It's the jelly bean problem with you as both researcher and subject: 15 outcomes tested monthly, the one significant mover gets a story. Over a year, you'll accumulate about 9 "breakthroughs," each credited to a different tweak, most of them weather.

The fix mirrors real research discipline: pick one or two primary metrics in advance, tied to the change you're testing, and judge only those, over a window set in advance. Let the other 13 be scenery. If the pre-chosen metric improves across the pre-set window, you have weak but real evidence. If you keep letting all 15 audition each month, you'll keep casting noise in the lead role — and spending money on its supplements.

I'm a careful driver — never had an accident in 15 years. I honestly believe my chance of a serious accident is basically zero. A friend who works in insurance says my own record is fooling me. Explain his side, with numbers.

His side starts with the reference class: not "me, specifically, feeling careful," but "drivers with my mileage and habits," because your personal sample is too small to measure a rare event. Fifteen accident-free years sounds like proof; run what it actually rules out.

Suppose drivers like you average a claim-worthy accident rate of about 1 per 100 driver-years (1% per year). Over 15 years, the chance of zero accidents is 0.99^15 ≈ 86%. So a perfectly average driver with your risk has an 86% chance of producing exactly your spotless record. Your record is what luck usually looks like — it barely distinguishes you from the average driver at all.

Now stretch the horizon the way insurance does. Over 40 years of driving at 1% per year, the chance of at least one accident is 1 - 0.99^40 ≈ 1 - 0.67 ≈ 33%. Even being genuinely 20% safer than average — 0.8% per year — leaves 1 - 0.992^40 ≈ 27% over a driving lifetime. "Basically zero" isn't available at any plausible level of carefulness; small annual risks compound into substantial lifetime ones.

The self-deception is using your inside view (fifteen calm years, felt control) in place of the outside view (the base rate of your reference class). The calm years are real but nearly uninformative about a 1-in-100 annual event — you'd need centuries of personal driving to measure your own rate. Price your risk from the class you belong to, then let your carefulness adjust it modestly. That's not pessimism; it's how your friend's industry stays solvent.
